   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis document covers California Assembly Bill 1305 as chaptered: «Assembly Bill No. 1305 CHAPTER 365 An act to add Part 10 (commencing with Section 44475) to Division 26 of the Health and Safety Code, relating to carbon offsets.» The stored title calls it the Voluntary Carbon Market Disclosures Act; the capture names the bill «AB-1305 Voluntary carbon market disclosures.» and the new Part «PART 10. Voluntary Carbon Market Disclosures», and holds no act title of that name. The claim provisions reach only an entity that both operates within the state and makes claims within it: «This section does not apply to entities that either do not operate within the state, or that do not make claims within the state.» What the text sets is quoted from the text; what it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:*, and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe Legislative Counsel's digest sums up the law: «This bill would require a business entity that is marketing or selling voluntary carbon offsets, as defined, within the state to disclose on the business entity’s internet website specified information about the applicable carbon offset project». It reaches buyers and claim-makers too: «The bill would also require an entity that purchases or uses voluntary carbon offsets that makes claims regarding the achievement of net zero emissions or other, similar claims, as specified, to disclose on the entity’s internet website specified information.» The text records how it became law: «Approved by Governor October 07, 2023. Filed with Secretary of State October 07, 2023.» The pages held give no entry-into-force date for the regulation; October 07, 2023 is the approval and filing date.\n\n*Analytical inference:* a freight business meets this law if it sells or markets offsets, buys offsets and makes a claim, or makes a net zero or carbon neutral claim about itself or a product, and does so within California. This rests on the three duties quoted in section 8.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: the Act's duties are stated without a calendar date, and the one recurring step is that «Disclosures pursuant to this part shall be updated no less than annually.» No deadline for a freight business falls within the coming weeks. A violation is costly, though: «a civil penalty of not more than two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500) per day».\n\n- A marketing lead lists, before the next campaign or tender response, every page, quote template and brochure that says net zero or carbon neutral about the business or a shipping product, because each such claim brings the disclosure duty quoted in section 8.\n- A compliance lead sets a yearly calendar entry to review each posted disclosure against its source documents, because the text requires an update no less than annually.\n- An operations lead, for any shipping product sold with offsets, records for each offset project the registry, the project identification number, the project name, the project type and the protocol, because the text requires those entries to be posted on the entity's website.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the three steps rest on the claim and disclosure duties and the annual update quoted in section 8; the text sets them on the entity that makes the claim, whatever its trade. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a particular product description counts as a claim under the Act, and whether the business operates within the state.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe text names these parties: the business entity that sells or markets offsets, «A business entity that is marketing or selling voluntary carbon offsets within the state»; the entity that buys or uses offsets and makes claims; the entity that makes claims, whether or not it buys offsets; and the offset project operator, in the definition of durability. Enforcement is by public lawyers: the penalty is «assessed and recovered in a civil action brought in the name of the people of the State of California by the Attorney General or by a district attorney, county counsel, or city attorney in a court of competent jurisdiction».\n\nThe text names no freight forwarder, carrier or shipper, and states no duty on a logistics provider as such.\n\n*Analytical inference:* a forwarder sits in the chain as the entity that makes the claim when it describes its own service or a product as carbon neutral or net zero, and as a buyer of offsets if it buys them to support that claim; the claim provisions extend to a claim about «a product». *Legal Confirmation Required:* which of the three roles a forwarder holds for a given product, and whether a customer-facing claim made by a carrier it books is the carrier's claim or the forwarder's.\n\n## 7. Threshold Questions\n\nThe first threshold question is what counts as an offset: «means any product sold or marketed in the state that claims to be a “greenhouse gas emissions offset,” a “voluntary emissions reduction,” a “retail offset,” or any like term, that connotes that the product represents or corresponds to a reduction in the amount of greenhouse gases present in the atmosphere or that prevents the emission of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere that would have otherwise been emitted.» The definition excludes mandated products: «does not include products that represent or correspond to legal or regulatory mandates for either of the following». The second is where the Act applies: «This section does not apply to entities that do not operate within the state or do not purchase or use voluntary carbon offsets sold within the state.» And for claim-makers: «This section does not apply to entities that either do not operate within the state, or that do not make claims within the state.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* an allowance bought under a mandatory emissions scheme falls outside the definition, while a voluntary offset sold with a shipping product falls inside it. *Legal Confirmation Required:* what operating within the state means for a forwarder with no California office, and where a claim is made when a website is read in California.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nSellers. «A business entity that is marketing or selling voluntary carbon offsets within the state shall disclose on the business entity’s internet website all of the following information». The list covers the protocol used, the project site, timeline and type, and «Whether there is independent expert or third-party validation or verification of the project attributes.» It adds «details regarding accountability measures if a project is not completed or does not meet the projected emissions reductions or removal benefits» and «The pertinent data and calculation methods needed to independently reproduce and verify the number of emissions reduction or removal credits issued using the protocol.»\n\nBuyers who make claims. «makes claims regarding the achievement of net zero emissions, claims that the entity, related entity, or a product is “carbon neutral,” or makes other claims implying the entity, related entity, or a product does not add net carbon dioxide or greenhouse gases to the climate or has made significant reductions to its carbon dioxide or greenhouse gas emissions shall disclose on the entity’s internet website all of the following information pertaining to each project or program». The list includes the seller's name, the registry or program, the project identification number, the project name, the project type, the protocol and «Whether there is independent third-party verification of company data and claims listed.» The section has a limit: «This section does not apply to entities that do not operate within the state or do not purchase or use voluntary carbon offsets sold within the state.»\n\nAnyone who makes claims. «An entity that makes claims regarding the achievement of net zero emissions, claims that the entity, a related or affiliated entity, or a product is “carbon neutral,” or makes other claims implying the entity, related or affiliated entity, or a product does not add net carbon dioxide or greenhouse gases, as defined in Section 38505, to the climate or has made significant reductions to its carbon dioxide or greenhouse gas emissions, as described in Section 38505, shall disclose on the entity’s internet website all of the following information pertaining to all greenhouse gas emissions associated with its claims». It must disclose «All information documenting how, if at all, a “carbon neutral,” “net zero emission,” or other similar claim was determined to be accurate or actually accomplished, and how interim progress toward that goal is being measured.» and «whether there is independent third-party verification of the company data and claims listed.»\n\nUpdating. «Disclosures pursuant to this part shall be updated no less than annually.»\n\nPenalty. «A person who violates this part is subject to a civil penalty of not more than two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500) per day, for each day that information is not available or is inaccurate on the person’s internet website, for each violation, not to exceed a total amount of five hundred thousand dollars ($500,000)».\n\n*Analytical inference:* the penalty runs per day that information is missing or inaccurate, so a claim left on a website without its disclosure keeps adding to the exposure up to the cap; the text states no pass-through of the penalty and no cost for the disclosure. *Legal Confirmation Required:* how the per day count applies to a claim repeated across several pages, which the text does not say.\n\nNo phase-in is stated in Sections 44475 to 44475.3 of the Health and Safety Code.\n\nObligations surveyed: 5; workspace-adjacent: 3; extracted as FACT: 11.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nThe reporting duty is a public website posting, not a filing: the entity must «disclose on the entity’s internet website» the listed information, and it must be refreshed: «Disclosures pursuant to this part shall be updated no less than annually.» The text states no registration with a state body and no report to an agency.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the data a business must collect is project-level offset detail for each offset and, for claims, the working that shows the claim was accurate; the text sets no format for the posting beyond the listed items. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a posting on a customer portal rather than a public page meets the website duty.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the system work is the claiming entity's. It must keep, for an offset it sells, the data needed so that a reader can «independently reproduce and verify the number of emissions reduction or removal credits issued using the protocol», and for a durability shorter than carbon dioxide's it must post «The durability period for any project that the seller knows or should know that the durability of the project’s greenhouse gas reductions or greenhouse gas removal enhancements is less than the atmospheric lifetime of carbon dioxide emissions.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* for a forwarder that sells a carbon-neutral shipping product with offsets, the gap is a product file that holds the offset registry entry, protocol and verification statement for each shipment batch, so the disclosure can be built and refreshed each year. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether offsets bought in bulk and applied to many shipments need a project entry for each.\n\n## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases\n\nThree limits narrow the duty: mandated products are outside the offset definition, as quoted in section 7; an entity that does not operate or make claims within the state is outside the claim provisions; and the claim-maker's proof is open-ended: «This information may include, but not be limited to, disclosure of independent third-party verification of all of the entity’s greenhouse gas emissions, identification of the entity’s science-based targets for its emissions reduction pathway».\n\n*Analytical inference:* the text lists third-party verification and science-based targets as examples of proof, not as required forms, so a claim-maker has latitude in how it shows a claim was accurate. *Legal Confirmation Required:* what proof would satisfy a prosecutor that a claim was determined to be accurate.\n\n## 14.    "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis brief covers the Energy Act 2023, a United Kingdom Public General Act published on legislation.gov.uk and headed «Energy Act 2023 2023 CHAPTER 52». Its long title begins: «An Act to make provision about energy production and security and the regulation of the energy market, including provision about the licensing of carbon dioxide transport and storage;»\n\nThe Act extends in two groups. «The following provisions extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, subject to subsection (5) — (a) Part 1 , except Chapter 4 ; (b) Part 2 ;» «The following provisions extend to England and Wales and Scotland only, subject to subsection (5) — (a) Chapter 4 of Part 1 ; (b) Part 3 ;»\n\nThe Act is long and mostly enabling: much of it lets the Secretary of State make regulations later. What it requires is quoted from its own text. What it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:*, and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*. A freight forwarder is not named in the Act.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe Act is a toolkit of licences, levies, powers and penalties for the energy sector. Four parts reach a freight business through its clients.\n\nCarbon dioxide transport and storage is licensed. «It is an offence for a person to carry on an activity within subsection (2) unless the person is authorised to do so by a licence.» The licensable activities are: «(2) The activities are— (a) operating a site for the disposal of carbon dioxide by way of geological storage; (b) providing a service of transporting carbon dioxide by a licensable means of transportation.»\n\nFuel movement is covered by Part 12, which is about keeping fuel supply running. Among the activities it covers are: «(c) the carriage of oil or renewable transport fuel by sea or inland water; (d) transporting oil or renewable transport fuel by road or rail;»\n\nGas shippers can be made to pay into a hydrogen levy, set out in section 4. Powers on the energy performance of premises and on marine oil pollution plans are covered in sections 8 and 11.\n\nThe Act does not start on one date. «(2) The following provisions come into force on the day on which this Act is passed» «(3) The following provisions come into force at the end of the period of 2 months beginning with the day on which this Act is passed— (a) Part 1 ; (b) Chapters 1 to 3 , 5 and 6 of Part 2 , so far as not already in force by virtue of subsection (2) ; (c) Part 3 ;»\n\n*Analytical inference:* because the Act enters into force in stages, each duty has to be checked against its own commencement note; section 14 lists the dates the text states.\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* which commencement group each duty in the Act belongs to and whether a later commencement order changes a duty described here.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: nothing in the Act sets a dated step that a freight forwarder must take, so the work now is to find which clients the Act reaches and to put one question to each.\n\n- A compliance lead asks each client that stores, handles, carries or transports oil or renewable transport fuel in the United Kingdom, at its next account review, whether its fuel tonnage in the last calendar year passed the 1,000 tonne threshold for information notices or the 500,000 tonne threshold for directions, both quoted in section 8.\n- A sales lead asks each client that holds a gas shipper licence, at its next account review, whether it has been told of any payment into the hydrogen levy, and records the answer, because the Act itself sets no rate.\n\n*Analytical inference:* both questions rest on the section 273 and section 269 spans quoted in section 8 and the section 70 span quoted in section 4; the Act itself puts those duties on the client and does not name a forwarder, but regulations under Part 11 may impose requirements on any person (section 8). *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a client's duty under these sections can be passed to a forwarder through the client's contract.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe Act names its parties by role, and a freight forwarder is not among them. The roles closest to freight are these.\n\nCore fuel sector participants: «“ core fuel sector participant ” means— (a) a person carrying on core fuel sector activities; (b) a Part 12 facility owner.» A wetstock manager is named separately: «“ relevant wetstock manager ” means a person who provides to persons who make retail supplies of core fuels in the United Kingdom stock management services in respect of such supplies.»\n\nGas shippers: «“ GB gas shipper ” means a person who holds a licence under section 7A(2) of the Gas Act 1986;» The levy duties fall on a defined group: «In this Chapter “ relevant market participants ” means one or more descriptions of persons specified in revenue support regulations, but a description so specified may not include persons other than— (a) GB gas shippers; (b) Northern Ireland gas shippers.»\n\nCarbon storage licensees and exploration operators are the parties of the information duties in section 10.\n\n*Analytical inference:* a forwarder meets the Act when a client holds one of these roles; the Act puts the duty on that role. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which role a client holds for a given movement of fuel, and whether arranging the carriage of fuel for a client falls within the core fuel sector activities listed in section 2.\n\n## 6. Threshold Questions\n\nThe thresholds in section 8 turn on one question: how a business's tonnage is counted. «a business “has capacity in excess of” a specified number of tonnes if in the most recently ended calendar year core fuel sector activities were carried on in that business in relation to more than that number of tonnes of core fuel;»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the count is made on the business that carries on the fuel activity, over the most recently ended calendar year, so a client's own figure decides whether it is inside the thresholds, not the volume a forwarder books for it. *Legal Confirmation Required:* how a client counts fuel that passes through several parties.\n\n## 8. (c) on conviction on indictment, to a fine.»\n\nPenalties on licence holders. «Where the economic regulator is satisfied that a licence holder has contravened or is contravening any relevant condition or requirement, the economic regulator may, subject to paragraph 6 , impose on the licence holder a penalty of such amount as is reasonable in all the circumstances of the case.» «The maximum amount of penalty that may be imposed on a licence holder in respect of a contravention may not exceed 10 per cent of the licence holder’s turnover.»\n\nFinancial penalties under carbon storage licences. «The financial penalty payable under a financial penalty notice in respect of a failure to comply with a sanctionable requirement (whether payable by one person, or jointly by two or more persons) must not exceed £1 million.» «The period specified under subsection (1) (c) (ii) must not end earlier than the end of the period of 28 days beginning with the day on which the financial penalty notice is given.»\n\nCore fuel sector directions. «The Secretary of State may, for the purpose of maintaining or improving core fuel sector resilience, direct a person to whom this section applies to do anything in relation to the person’s relevant activities or assets (for example, to acquire and install specific equipment, or carry out specific works, at the person’s own expense).» «This section applies to the following persons— (a) a person carrying on core fuel sector activities in the course of a business which has capacity in excess of 500,000 tonnes; (b) a Part 12 facility owner if the owned facility has capacity in excess of 20,000 tonnes.» Not complying is an offence: «Any person who, without reasonable excuse, fails to comply with a direction given to the person under section 269 commits an offence and is liable— (a) on summary conviction in England and Wales, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding the general limit in a magistrates’ court or a fine (or both);» «(d) on conviction on indictment, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 2 years or a fine (or both).»\n\nInformation from fuel businesses. «The Secretary of State may by notice in writing require any of the following to provide the Secretary of State with information relating to their relevant activities or assets— (a) a person carrying on core fuel sector activities in the course of a business which has capacity in excess of 1,000 tonnes; (b) a Part 12 facility owner whose owned facility has capacity in excess of 1,000 tonnes.»\n\nHydrogen levy. «Revenue support regulations may make provision for relevant market participants (see subsection (8) ) to make payments to a hydrogen levy administrator for the purpose of enabling— (a) a hydrogen transport counterparty to make payments under a hydrogen transport revenue support contract» «Revenue support regulations may make provision about eligibility for exemptions from obligations imposed on relevant market participants by regulations within subsections (1) to (4) .» «Revenue support regulations may make provision imposing on a relevant market participant who receives a payment from a hydrogen levy administrator or a relevant counterparty a requirement to secure that customers of the relevant market participant receive, by a time specified in the regulations, such benefit from the payment as may be specified in or determined in accordance with the regulations.»\n\nEnergy performance of premises. «Energy performance regulations may provide for the imposition of civil penalties by enforcement authorities in relation to cases falling within subsection (1) (b) , (c) or (d) ; but the regulations may not provide for a civil penalty that exceeds £15,000.»\n\nEnergy savings schemes. «ESOS regulations may— (a) impose requirements on any person;»\n\nMarine oil pollution plans. «(8) Regulations under subsection (1) or (5) may not provide— (a) for a criminal offence to be punishable with imprisonment; (b) for a civil penalty to exceed £50,000.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* each duty above sits on a licence holder, a fuel business, a gas shipper or a person responsible for the infrastructure named; none is placed on a forwarder by the Act's own text, although regulations under Part 11 may impose requirements on any person, and the Act states no step by which a cost of these duties reaches a customer's price. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nCarbon storage licensees and exploration operators must name a contact person: «A person within subsection (2) (a “relevant person”) must— (a) appoint an individual to act as an information and samples coordinator, and (b) notify the OGA of that individual’s name and contact details.» «The following persons are within this subsection— (a) a licensee, and (b) an exploration operator under a carbon storage licence.» The change duty follows: «The relevant person must notify the OGA of any change in the identity or contact details of the information and samples coordinator within a reasonable period of the change taking place.»\n\nMarine oil pollution regulations may also require incident reports: «in connection with that requirement, and (c) about the reporting of such incidents.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* these registration and report duties fall on licensees, exploration operators and the persons responsible for the infrastructure; none is placed on a forwarder by the Act's own text; regulations under Part 11 may impose requirements on any person (section 8).\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a client's information duty reaches a forwarder acting for it.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the Act builds no system for a freight forwarder. A client in the fuel classes may have to build two things, and an operations lead asks each such client, at its next account review, who would answer a notice and how often it could supply tonnage.\n\nInformation notices can set the rhythm of reporting: «A notice under subsection (1) or (2) may— (a) specify the manner in which information is to be provided; (b) specify time limits for providing information; (c) require information to be provided at specified intervals.» Regulations may require emergency plans for places that handle or store oil, including a harbour: «requiring a person responsible for infrastructure or a place to which subsection (2) applies to have an emergency plan setting out arrangements for responding to incidents which cause, or may cause, marine oil pollution» «(c) a harbour; (d) a facility, that is not offshore, for handling or storing oil or gas;»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a client that handles fuel in a harbour or a handling facility may need an emergency plan and a way to report at intervals; the Act sets neither for a forwarder. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that uses such a facility for a client must supply data to the client or the Secretary of State.\n\n## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases\n\nTwo limits on scope are stated. «In subsection (2) the references to “oil” do not include crude oil which has not yet entered any refinery or terminal in the United Kingdom.» Licensing has its own carve-out: «For the purposes of this Part activities are “licensable activities” if undertaking them without the authority of a licence or exemption constitutes an offence under section 2 (1) .»\n\n*Analytical inference:* fuel that has not yet entered a refinery or terminal in the United Kingdom is outside the fuel activity list, so a movement of that fuel is not by itself a core fuel sector activity. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a client's product is crude oil within this exclusion.\n\n## 14.    "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis document covers CountEmissionsEU, the European Union rule for measuring and communicating the greenhouse gas emissions of freight and passenger transport services. The path to adoption, in the sources' words: the proposal, «On 11 July 2023, the Commission tabled a legislative proposal on an EU-wide framework (CountEmissionsEU) for harmonised measurement of emissions from transport and logistics services.»; the Council position, «Council adopts its position on the accounting of greenhouse gas emissions of transport services , Press release, 4 December 2023»; Parliament's first report, «It was voted on in plenary on 10 April 2024.»; the provisional agreement, approved by two Parliament committees «On 4 December 2025»; and the second reading, «The TRAN committee vote in second reading took place on 17 March 2026.» The tracker lists the final act: «Regulation (EU) 2026/1030 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2026 on the greenhouse gas emissions accounting of transport services». The captured texts hold the Commission's 2023 proposal, the Parliament's tracker page and a Commission news item of 6 November 2025, but not the text of the adopted regulation, so each article quoted below is the Commission's proposed wording and is marked as such; the tracker says the agreed text changed it. The jurisdiction is the European Union, and the proposal states its reach: «This Regulation establishes rules for the accounting of the greenhouse gas emissions of transport services that start or end on the Union territory.» What the texts say is stated from their own wording; what it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:* and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nIn plain terms, the regulation is about how a transport emissions figure is made and shown to a customer, and it gives one method for it. The tracker describes it: «The proposed regulation establishes a single, voluntary EU methodology for the measurement of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from both freight and passenger transport.» Its aim: «A harmonised system would help consumers and businesses choose transport services based on their environmental performance and reduce the risk of greenwashing.» The Commission's news item adds: «The framework is based on an internationally recognised methodology (EN ISO 14083:2023).» It frames the aim as «helping the sector to contribute to the target of cutting transport emissions by 90% by 2050».\n\nIt is a rule about how emissions figures are made and shown, not a cap or a charge. The reach is set by who publishes: «The regulation will apply to companies that choose to publish emissions from their activities.» The proposal's scope article says: «This Regulation applies to any entity providing or organising freight and passenger services in the Union that calculates greenhouse gas emissions of a transport service starting or ending on the Union territory and discloses disaggregated information on those emissions to any third party for commercial or regulatory purposes.» The tracker also says the method can reach beyond the Union: «This would allow the proposed regulation to also be applied to transport chains which are partly outside the EU.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a forwarder or carrier that organises freight services and gives a customer a per-service emissions figure falls within the wording of the scope article quoted from the proposal. One that gives no such figure is outside it on that wording. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the adopted Regulation (EU) 2026/1030 keeps the proposal's scope wording, and whether a particular customer statement counts as disclosure for commercial purposes.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: the regulation applies 48 months after it enters into force, so no step is due within the next 30 days. A sustainability data lead lists, at the next customer-reporting cycle, each transport emissions figure the business gives to customers, and records for each whether it follows EN ISO 14083:2023, the method the Commission names as the base of the framework.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the step rests on the sentences «The framework is based on an internationally recognised methodology (EN ISO 14083:2023).» and «The regulation will apply to companies that choose to publish emissions from their activities.»; the texts state no date by which a business must switch method, only the application period quoted in section 8. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the adopted article on the method and on which firms are in scope, which the captured texts do not hold.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe proposal names these roles: the entity that calculates and discloses emissions, called a concerned entity; the data intermediary, defined as a party that «means a legal or natural person collecting and disclosing information on greenhouse gas emissions of a transport service on the basis of separate legal, contractual or other relevant arrangements»; the conformity assessment body that verifies; and the Commission with the European Environment Agency, which builds the databases. The scope article names the entity that provides or organises freight services.\n\n*Analytical inference:* a forwarder that organises a freight service and gives its customer the emissions figure holds the concerned-entity role on the proposal's wording; a platform or software supplier that collects and passes on such figures for others fits the data intermediary definition. The texts name no customs broker and no shipper. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which role the business holds for each service it quotes, and whether the adopted text keeps these roles.\n\n## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events\n\nThe Commission lists work still to come: «After the final adoption, the Commission will work with the EEA to set up the databases and the free calculation tool for SMEs. It will also adopt the necessary delegated and implementing acts to detail technical specifications, certification and verification rules.» The news item names two free tools: «Transport operators will also have access to a free calculation tool to support ease of use, while certified external tools are allowed to encourage innovation.» No date for these acts or databases is stated in the captured texts.\n\n*Analytical inference:* technical specifications and verification rules are set in later acts, so the detail of how a figure must be calculated and verified is not final in the captured texts. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which implementing and delegated acts have been adopted since the news item.\n\n## 7. Threshold Questions\n\nThe question that decides whether the regulation bites is whether the business calculates the emissions of a transport service and discloses disaggregated information to a third party: «This Regulation applies to any entity providing or organising freight and passenger services in the Union that calculates greenhouse gas emissions of a transport service starting or ending on the Union territory and discloses disaggregated information on those emissions to any third party for commercial or regulatory purposes.» The Commission's news item reads the same way: «The regulation will apply to companies that choose to publish emissions from their activities.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the gate is publication to a third party, not the size or mode of the business. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a figure given to a customer on request, as opposed to one published, counts as disclosure.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nScope. In the Commission's 2023 proposal: «This Regulation applies to any entity providing or organising freight and passenger services in the Union that calculates greenhouse gas emissions of a transport service starting or ending on the Union territory and discloses disaggregated information on those emissions to any third party for commercial or regulatory purposes.»\n\nMethod. In the proposal: «The greenhouse gas emissions of transport services shall be calculated on the basis of the method ology defined in EN ISO 14083 :2023 standard , in its up-to-date version , and the rules set out in Chapter III of this Regulation.» The tracker confirms the standard as the base: the agreed text «anchors the methodology more explicitly in the ISO standard».\n\nData. In the proposal: «Entities referred to in Article 2 shall prioriti s e the use of primary data for calculating greenhouse gas emissions of a transport service.» The minimum figure for freight is set in the proposal: «(a) mass CO2e per tonne kilometre, or equivalent units, for freight transport;»\n\nDisclosure. In the proposal: «Concerned entities shall disclose output data in a clear and unambiguous manner .» Free default values are promised: «Access to the database referred to in paragraph 1 , to consult or use default emission intensity values shall be open to the public and free of charge.»\n\nVerification. In the proposal: «Output data referred to in Article 9 shall be subject to verification of its conformity with the requirements laid down in Articles 4 to 9 of this Regulation.» The proposal excludes small firms: «The verification requirements referred to in paragraph 1 shall apply to concerned entities referred to Article 2, with the exception of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises referred to in Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC 66 .» The news item agrees: «Larger companies will need to verify their data, while smaller firms are exempt, to reduce unnecessary burdens.»\n\nChanges in the agreed text. The tracker lists: «clearer scope and proportionality: obligations are phased in and adjusted to avoid disproportionate burdens, especially for SMEs and small operators» and «clarification that emissions information is for transparency and information purposes only, with explicit safeguards against misuse regarding pricing, taxation, or contractual liability»\n\nEntry into force. The Commission's news item, «Publication date 6 November 2025», says the adopted regulation is one «which will enter into force 20 days after publication in the Official Journal of the EU». The final act was published on 12 May 2026: «On 28 April 2026, the plenary adopted the provisional agreement, the final act was signed on 29 April 2026. The final act was published on 12 May 2026.»\n\nApplication. «The regulation’s provisions will be implemented 48 months after entry into force.»\n\nNo penalty, fine or sanction is stated in the captured texts, so what a business risks if non-compliant is not stated.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the tracker says emissions information is for transparency and information purposes only, with safeguards against misuse regarding pricing, taxation or contractual liability; the texts state no pass-through of any cost of the method to a customer. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the adopted article on those safeguards and on each duty above, since the quoted articles are the proposal's wording and the agreed text changed them.\n\nObligations surveyed: 9; workspace-adjacent: 4; extracted as FACT: 18.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nThe proposal sets evidence and list duties. A concerned entity keeps evidence: «Concerned entities shall be able to establish evidence substantiating how the output data w ere established» The verifier reports a yearly list: «By 31 March each year, the conformity assessment body shall notify that list to the Commission.» The tracker says the agreed text keeps a verification layer, and the Commission's news item says larger companies verify their data.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the list duty falls on the conformity assessment body, not on the business that is verified. No registration step for a freight business is stated in the captured texts. *Legal Confirmation Required:* what evidence the adopted text asks a concerned entity to keep and for how long.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the proposal asks entities to use measured data first and allows default values only as a fallback, so the data a business holds decides how it can calculate. A data-systems lead checks, before the 48 month application period ends, whether the shipment records can supply measured fuel or energy use for each leg of a service, and lists the legs that would have to use the public default values.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the step rests on the primary data sentence «Entities referred to in Article 2 shall prioriti s e the use of primary data for calculating greenhouse gas emissions of a transport service.» and the free default values sentence «Access to the database referred to in paragraph 1 , to consult or use default emission intensity values shall be open to the public and free of charge.». *Legal Confirmation Required:* the adopted article on primary data and defaults, which the captured texts do not hold.\n\n## 12.    "item_id": "7dabbe8a-2ba9-4242-8a51-57495e56993f",

   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis brief covers a European Union implementing regulation on the carbon border adjustment mechanism (the CBAM): «COMMISSION IMPLEMENTING REGULATION (EU) 2025/2621 of 16 December 2025 laying down rules for the application of Regulation (EU) 2023/956 of the European Parliament and the Council as regards the establishment of default values (Text with EEA relevance)» It was published in the Official Journal and it is binding on every Member State: «This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.»\n\nIt sets the default values to be used where embedded emissions are determined on the basis of default values under the CBAM Regulation. What it requires is quoted from its own text. What it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:*, and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*. A freight forwarder is not named in the Regulation.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe CBAM Regulation requires default values to be used in some cases: «(1) Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2023/956 requires the use of default values for determining embedded emissions in goods other than electricity and in imported electricity , and for determining indirect embedded emissions .» This Regulation lays those values down. Its design rule is conservative: «Therefore, the default values including mark-ups should be determined using a conservative approach that ensures that embedded emissions are not underestimated when applying default values.»\n\nThe mark-up on each default value is raised in steps so that prices are not hit at once: «To avoid immediate disproportionate impacts on prices of goods, and to give economic operators time to adapt, the mark-up should be gradually phased-in.» Declarants may use defaults at first and rely on actual data later: «CBAM declarants should therefore be able to use default values in those first years, and rely on actual emissions subsequently.»\n\nWhen it takes effect: «This Regulation shall enter into force on the third day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .» The Regulation enters into force on that day, and the date from which the values must be used is: «It shall apply from 1 January 2026.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* because the values carry a rising mark-up, an importer that relies on defaults for the same good declares a higher figure in each later year, as the tables in section 8 show; the text states no price for the resulting CBAM certificates.\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* which of the Regulation's cases (goods, indirect emissions, electricity, unknown precursor country) applies to a given import and whether a revision changes it.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nCOST ALERT: default values carry a mark-up that rises by step, so a declaration built on default values rises in each later year. In the table for cement the mark-up reads 10 % for 2026, 20 % for 2027 and 30 % from 2028 onwards, and the fertiliser table holds 1 % throughout (section 8).\n\n- A trade-compliance lead asks each importer client, for every good and country of production the client plans to import in 2027, at its next onboarding review and before its first 2027 declaration, whether it will declare actual emissions or fall back on default values, and for default values which annex applies: Annex I for goods, Annex II for indirect emissions, Annex III for electricity, Annex IV for a precursor whose country of production cannot be identified.\n- A client-contract lead notes against each such client the revision date, December 2027 at the latest, as the point where the default values and mark-ups can change, and asks the client to refresh its declaration basis then.\n\n*Analytical inference:* both steps rest on the annex rules and the mark-up columns quoted in section 8 and on the revision text in section 6; the Regulation puts the use of default values on the party that determines embedded emissions, not on a forwarder. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that prepares data for an importer carries any duty for the choice between actual and default values.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe Regulation speaks of importers, CBAM declarants and economic operators, and a freight forwarder is not named. Declarants may use defaults in the first years: «and hence CBAM declarants should therefore be able to use default values in those first years, and rely on actual emissions subsequently.» A precursor whose country of production is unknown carries the worst case: «where the country of production of a precursor cannot be identified, the default value to be used for that precursor should be the default value of the third country with the highest emission intensities for that precursor.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a client that cannot name the country of production of a precursor is treated as if it came from the highest-emitting country, so supplier records decide the figure a client declares. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which party must show the country of production for a precursor and whether a forwarder's records can serve that purpose.\n\n## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events\n\nThe Regulation is meant to be replaced. Consultation: «Where the Commission proceeds to revise this Implementing Act, it should conduct a public consultation to uphold transparency and to ensure a meaningful participation of all relevant stakeholders, in accordance with the Commission’s Better Regulation Guidelines.» Timing: «The default values and mark-ups shall be revised by December 2027 at the latest.» «The Commission should make all necessary efforts, in close collaboration with the Member States and based on a systematic and holistic review, to ensure that a revision of the default values can already be carried out in 2026.» The operative article says: «It shall be revised in 2027 at the latest.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the revision may come before the December 2027 limit, since the recital asks for efforts to revise in 2026, so a client's declaration basis can change inside the period shown for the mark-up steps. *Legal Confirmation Required:* what revised values and mark-ups will apply to goods imported before the revision.\n\n## 7. Threshold Questions\n\nTwo threshold questions decide which table a good uses. First, the country: «Where a country or territory is not explicitly listed, the default value for the respective good from the table ‘Other countries and territories’ needs to be selected. Where a country or territory is explicitly listed but no value is provided or the relevant field shows ‘–’, the default value for the respective good from the table ‘Other countries and territories’ needs to be selected.» Second, a precursor: «By way of derogation from paragraph 2, where a country of production cannot be identified for a precursor, the default values laid down in Annex IV shall be used.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a good from a country that is missing from a table, or has a dash in its field, takes the other-countries table value; a precursor with an unidentified country takes Annex IV. *Legal Confirmation Required:* how a country of production is shown for a given good.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nWhich annex applies. «Where the embedded emissions in imported goods are determined on the basis of default values in accordance with Article 7(2), point (b), of Regulation (EU) 2023/956, the default values laid down in Annex I to this Regulation shall be used.» «Where the embedded emissions of complex goods are determined on the basis of actual values, and the embedded emissions of precursors used in the production of those complex goods are determined on the basis of default values in accordance with Article 15 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2547 ( 2 ) , the default values laid down in Annex I shall be used for those precursors.» «Where the specific indirect embedded emissions are determined on the basis of default values in accordance with Article 7(4) of Regulation (EU) 2023/956, the default values laid down in Annex II to this Regulation shall be used.» «Where the embedded direct emissions in electricity imported into the customs territory of the Union are determined on the basis of default values in accordance with Article 7(3) of Regulation (EU) 2023/956, the default values laid down in Annex III to this Regulation shall be used.»\n\nThe Annex I title: «ANNEX I Default values for goods imported into the customs territory of the Union, except for electricity»\n\nThe mark-up steps. «2026 Default Value (including mark-up) 2027 Default Value (including mark-up) 2028 and onwards Default Value (including mark-up) Underlying production route determining CBAM BM Cement 10 % mark-up 20 % mark-up 30 % mark-up» A worked row from the other-countries table: «2523 10 00 Grey clinker 1,370 0,050 1,410 1,551 1,692 1,833 (A)»\n\nPenalty. This Regulation states no penalty, fine or enforcement consequence.\n\n*Analytical inference:* each rule above tells the party determining embedded emissions which table to use; none states a charge to a customer, and the numbers in the row rise with the mark-up step. No phase-in is stated in Articles 1 and 2 beyond the mark-up columns of the annexes. No scope limit is stated in Articles 1 and 2 beyond the cases each paragraph names.\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder's customer data choices affect which annex applies, and which table applies to a good whose country of production is only partly known.\n\nObligations surveyed: 6; workspace-adjacent: 2; extracted as FACT: 7.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nThe Regulation sets values, not a filing. The values link to two other implementing acts. For the free allocation adjustment: «the specific embedded free allocation shall be based on the corresponding underlying production route determining the CBAM benchmark (BM) as defined in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2620 ( 1 ) on the calculation of the free allocation adjustment to the number of CBAM certificates to be surrendered.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the reporting steps sit in the acts the annexes name, not in this Regulation; the text read here names no registration for a forwarder. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which of those acts requires a record from a forwarder, if any.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nCOST ALERT: the Regulation requires no system of a freight forwarder, but a client that wants actual values instead of defaults has to hold supplier data. A data lead asks each importer client, at its next onboarding review, which of its goods lack a named country of production or a per-good emission figure, because for those the default tables apply: «Where a country or territory is explicitly listed but no value is provided or the relevant field shows ‘–’, the default value for the respective good from the table ‘Other countries and territories’ needs to be selected.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* where a table shows a dash for a country, the other-countries value is used, so missing supplier data moves a good to the table with its own values. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a client expects its forwarder to hold or pass on supplier emission data.\n\n## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases\n\nTwo edge points. The fertiliser sector has its own lower rate: «Specific considerations apply to the fertilisers sector where a lower mark-up should be applied.» «Fertilisers 1 % mark-up 1 % mark-up 1 % mark-up»\n\nThe Regulation also marks one exception to the order of annexes: «By way of derogation from paragraph 2, where a country of production cannot be identified for a precursor, the default values laid down in Annex IV shall be used.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a fertiliser import sees a smaller rise from the mark-up than cement, and a precursor with an unknown country is the one case that uses Annex IV. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which CN code row covers a given fertiliser or precursor.\n\n## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline\n\n- 16 December 2025: the Regulation is adopted; «Done at Brussels, 16 December 2025.»\n- 1 January 2026: the Regulation applies; the mark-up column for 2026 starts at 10 % for cement (in force)\n- 2027: the 20 % mark-up column applies; the Regulation is to be revised in 2027 at the latest (ahead)\n- December 2027: the default values and mark-ups are to be revised by this month at the latest (ahead)\n- 2028 and onwards: the 30 % mark-up column applies (ahead)\n*Analytical inference:* the first two dates are past; the rest are the Regulation's stated steps and may move if a revision comes earlier.\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the revision due by December 2027 changes the mark-up steps listed.\n\n## 15. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis document covers Norway's zero-emission requirement for passenger ships in the five World Heritage fjords, a new part of the environmental safety rules for ships. The Norwegian Maritime Authority (NMA) states the decision: «The Norwegian Government has decided to introduce zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords, effective from 1 January 2026 for passenger ships of less than 10,000 gross tonnage, and from 1 January 2032 for passenger ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards.» The rule is made as «as part of the Regulations of 30 May 2012 No. 488 on environmental safety for ships and mobile offshore units», and it is set out in a new section: «The zero-emission requirements are set out in a new section 10b of the Environmental Safety Regulations.» The regulation enters into force on 1 January 2026 for passenger ships under 10,000 gross tonnage and on 1 January 2032 for larger ones. It rests on a parliamentary decision: «the Storting's petition resolution No. 672 of 3 May 2018, which mandates the introduction of zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords by 2026». The circular is dated: «Date: 14 April 2025 Series RSR Number RSR 04 - 2025». The Lovdata record of the regulation lists the amendment: «10 april 2025 nr. 671 (i kraft 1 jan 2026)». The jurisdiction is Norway, and the fjords are named: «The requirements will apply to the five World Heritage fjords: Nærøyfjord, Aurlandsfjord, Geirangerfjord, Sunnylvsfjord, and Tafjord.» What the texts say is stated from their own wording; what it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:* and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe rule says what a ship in the fjords may burn. The NMA defines it: «The term zero emissions means that energy sources used must not result in direct emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) or methane (CH4).» The rule is technology-neutral: «The zero-emission requirement is formulated in a technology-neutral manner, with no specific prescriptions as to how it must be met.» It reaches ships by size and by date: «This requirement will apply from 2026 to passenger ships of less than 10,000 gross tonnage, and from 2032 to passenger ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards.» And it reaches every passenger ship in the area, passing or staying: «The zero-emission requirement set out in section 10b applies to all passenger ships while they are within the World Heritage fjords, regardless of whether they operate exclusively within the fjords or only partially transit through them.»\n\nThe text names the ship types it has in mind as cruise ships, ferries, high-speed craft and other tourist vessels. It says a passenger ship is one that carries over twelve people: «A passenger ship is defined as a vessel that may carry more than 12 passengers.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the rule is aimed at passenger ships and names no cargo ship, so a freight business meets it only when its cargo or its people travel on a ferry, cruise ship or other passenger ship through the fjords. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a ferry that carries road freight counts as a passenger ship under the definition quoted above.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: the requirement for passenger ships under 10,000 gross tonnage is already in force and the next dated steps lie in 2029 and 2032, so no step falls due within the next 30 days.\n\n- A route-planning lead checks, before booking any ferry or passenger-ship leg that passes through the five World Heritage fjords, whether the operator's ship meets the zero-emission requirement or holds an exemption, and records the answer in the booking file.\n- A fleet-planning lead asks each ocean or coastal carrier serving the fjords, at the next contract renewal, whether its cargo ships of 1000 gross tonnage or more will meet the NOx Tier III requirements that the regulation sets for cargo ships from 1 January 2030.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the first step rests on the scope sentence «The zero-emission requirement set out in section 10b applies to all passenger ships while they are within the World Heritage fjords, regardless of whether they operate exclusively within the fjords or only partially transit through them.» and the second on the cargo ship NOx sentence in section 8; the texts state no price or surcharge effect on a freight booking. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a ship on a given leg is a passenger ship and whether any exemption has been granted to it.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe texts name these roles: the passenger ship and its company, the shipping company that must ensure compliance, the NMA that supervises, the port that supplies shore power, and the Ministry of Climate and Environment on whose behalf the NMA acts. On responsibility the NMA says: «Although the requirements apply to individual ships, it is the company's responsibility to ensure compliance in accordance with section 4 of the Ship Safety and Security Act.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a forwarder, shipper or customs broker is not named, so on the texts' own wording the duty sits with the ship's company, not with the party who books a passage. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which party is the company for a ship a client books, and whether a booking contract passes any of the duty on.\n\n## 5. Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis\n\nThe NMA circular RSR 04-2025 comments on each paragraph of section 10b. On fuel for ignition: the third paragraph permits fuels needed to ignite the energy sources, such as pilot fuels. On nitrous oxide: «The fourth paragraph permits limited emissions of nitrous oxide (N₂O) resulting from the use of the energy sources specified in the first and second paragraphs.» On shore power, the NMA says: «Using shore power while ships are at berth could be an effective way to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from passenger ships in the World Heritage fjords.» The NMA also gave guidance on the older rules for the fjords, set by an earlier circular: «Date: 01 March 2019 Series RSR Number RSR 2 - 2019». On the environmental instruction for large ships it says: «According to new section 14d of the Environmental Safety Regulations, ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards operating in the World Heritage fjords must carry an environmental instruction that specifically describes the measures to ensure compliance with the requirements for operations in the World Heritage fjords.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the circular is the authority's own reading of the rule, so it shows how the NMA intends to apply it, but it is not the rule text. *Legal Confirmation Required:* what the NMA means by shore power being available to a ship, which the circular reads as compatible connection points on the ship and the port and a port able to supply the power.\n\n## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events\n\nThe circular names one point that may change the text: «Once such a framework is in place, the fourth paragraph may be revised to incorporate more detailed regulation of these specific emissions.» No date is stated for such a framework or for a revision.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the nitrous oxide paragraph is the part most likely to be rewritten, and the texts give no date. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the nitrous oxide paragraph has been revised since the circular of 14 April 2025.\n\n## 7. Threshold Questions\n\nThree questions decide whether the rule applies to a ship. Is it a passenger ship: «A passenger ship is defined as a vessel that may carry more than 12 passengers.» Is it inside the World Heritage fjords: «The requirements will apply to the five World Heritage fjords: Nærøyfjord, Aurlandsfjord, Geirangerfjord, Sunnylvsfjord, and Tafjord.» And how large is it: «This requirement will apply from 2026 to passenger ships of less than 10,000 gross tonnage, and from 2032 to passenger ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a ship that is not a passenger ship is outside section 10b on this wording, whatever its size. *Legal Confirmation Required:* how a ship that carries both passengers and freight is classed.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nDates. «This requirement will apply from 2026 to passenger ships of less than 10,000 gross tonnage, and from 2032 to passenger ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards.»\n\nZero emission. «The first paragraph of the provision stipulates that, from 1 January 2026, passenger ships of less than 10,000 gross tonnage operating in the World Heritage fjords shall use energy sources that do not result in direct emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) or methane (CH4).» «According to the second paragraph, from 1 January 2032, passenger ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards operating in the World Heritage fjords shall use energy sources that do not result in direct emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) or methane (CH4).»\n\nScope. «The zero-emission requirement set out in section 10b applies to all passenger ships while they are within the World Heritage fjords, regardless of whether they operate exclusively within the fjords or only partially transit through them.»\n\nBiogas. «Additionally, the Government has determined that passenger ships may use biogas as an alternative fuel, and that the use of shore power will be mandatory where such facilities are available.» «Biogas must be bunkered within the final month before the ship enters the World Heritage fjords, and the amount bunkered must correspond to the amount expected to be used during the voyage though the fjords.» «Biogas sourced from the gas grid, accompanied by a certificate based on a mass balance system, does not meet the requirements for operating in the World Heritage fjords.»\n\nShore power. «According to the seventh paragraph of the provision, passenger ships operating in the World Heritage fjords are required to use shore power where such facilities are available.»\n\nDocuments. «The eighth paragraph requires that ships carry documentation on board confirming compliance with the fuel-related requirements set out in this provision.»\n\nExemptions. «The Government has determined that there is a need for an exemption from the zero-emission requirements for passenger ships deployed in regular service due to planned roadworks or in response to emergency situations.» «The Government has decided that county-operated high-speed craft shall be exempt from the zero- emission requirements.»\n\nResponsibility and enforcement. «Although the requirements apply to individual ships, it is the company's responsibility to ensure compliance in accordance with section 4 of the Ship Safety and Security Act.» «The NMA may supervise compliance with the provision and, where necessary, implement administrative measures in accordance with chapter 8 of the Ship Safety and Security Act or impose violation fines pursuant to chapter 9.»\n\nOlder NOx step for passenger ships. «From 1 January 2025, stricter rules on NOx emissions have come into effect, requiring all passenger ships of more than 1,000 gross tonnage to comply with the NOx Tier III standard, pursuant to section 14c of the Environmental Safety Regulations and MARPOL Regulation VI/13.»\n\nLarger ships. «For passenger ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards, the zero-emission requirement does not enter into force until 1 January 2032.»\n\nCargo ships. The Lovdata text of the regulation sets a NOx step for cargo ships in the fjords: «Lasteskip med bruttotonnasje 1000 eller mer som seiler i verdensarvfjordene skal, uavhengig av kravene som gjaldt ved skipets byggeår, oppfylle Nivå III-kravene, jf. MARPOL regel VI/13, fra 1. januar 2030.»\n\nThe circular states no fine amount, so what a business risks if non-compliant is stated as administrative measures and violation fines only. The circular states no pass-through of any compliance cost to a freight rate or a passenger fare.\n\n*Analytical inference:* each duty above falls on the ship and its company; the texts state no cost to a customer of that company. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the amount of any violation fine under chapter 9 of the Ship Safety and Security Act, and whether a cost of compliance may be charged on to a client.\n\nObligations surveyed: 9; workspace-adjacent: 3; extracted as FACT: 19.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nThe reporting duty is documentary: «The eighth paragraph requires that ships carry documentation on board confirming compliance with the fuel-related requirements set out in this provision.» The circular adds that proof of fuel compliance is built from certificates and delivery notes, and that missing documents can lead to sanctions: «The NMA may supervise compliance with the provision and, where necessary, implement administrative measures in accordance with chapter 8 of the Ship Safety and Security Act or impose violation fines pursuant to chapter 9.» Exemptions are given by the NMA on application and last at most two years: «Exemptions may be granted for a maximum of two years at a time and, in any case, not beyond 31 December 2029.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* these duties fall on the ship's company. The texts state no registration step for a freight business. *Legal Confirmation Required:* what documents a ship must carry and for how long.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the system work sits with the ship operator, which needs shore power, charging access or a certified fuel supply. A procurement lead asks each ferry or cruise operator on a quoted itinerary, before accepting the booking, for confirmation of how the ship will meet the requirement in the fjords, shore power or battery or biogas with its documents, and files the reply with the booking.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the step rests on the NMA's remark that «In general, batteries represent a viable option for ships of less than 10,000 gross tonnage, and access to charging infrastructure will be a critical prerequisite for meeting the core zero-emission requirement.», and on the shore power and document sentences in section 8. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder has any duty to check a carrier's documents.\n\n## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases\n\nSeveral exemptions apply. For small ships there is a temporary route: «Exemptions may be granted for a maximum of two years at a time and, in any case, not beyond 31 December 2029.» And its conditions are limited: «the exemption applies to established vessels that were operating in the World Heritage fjords in 2024 and intend to continue operating there until 2030.» The circular adds for new entrants: «Any new operations must comply with the zero-emission requirements as of 1 January 2026.» Other exemptions: «The Government has determined that there is a need for an exemption from the zero-emission requirements for passenger ships deployed in regular service due to planned roadworks or in response to emergency situations.» «The Government has decided that county-operated high-speed craft shall be exempt from the zero- emission requirements.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* an older small ship that sails only in the fjords may hold an exemption until the end of 2029; a ship new to the fjords may not. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a particular ship has an exemption decision and for how long.\n\n## 13. Adjacent Industry Research and Alternatives\n\nThe rule was built next to EU fuel rules: «In developing the proposal for zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords, the NMA therefore aligned the specific requirements with the relevant EU legislation.» The Norwegian state has also paid for infrastructure: «The government has therefore allocated NOK 100 million in support to Aurland Port Authority in the 2025 state budget, which Enova has been given a special mandate to administer.»\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether an EU fuel rule applies to the same ship.\n\n## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline\n\n- 3 May 2018: the Storting's petition resolution No. 672 mandated zero-emission requirements in the World Heritage fjords by 2026 (past)\n- 01 March 2019: the NMA circular RSR 2-2019 set earlier rules for the fjords (past)\n- 10 April 2025: the amendment adding sections 10b and 10c was enacted (past)\n- 14 April 2025: the NMA circular RSR 04-2025 announced the zero-emission requirements (past)\n- 1 January 2025: the NOx Tier III step for passenger ships over 1,000 gross tonnage came into effect (past)\n- 1 January 2026: the zero-emission requirement applies to passenger ships under 10,000 gross tonnage (in force)\n- 31 December 2029: the latest date to which any temporary exemption for small passenger ships may run\n- 1 January 2030: NOx Tier III applies to cargo ships of 1000 gross tonnage or more in the fjords\n- 1 January 2032: the zero-emission requirement also applies to passenger ships of 10,000 gross tonnage and upwards\n\n*Analytical inference:* the rows give the dates the quoted texts state; the 2030 row comes from the Norwegian text of the regulation, which is the only capture to state it. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the current dates in the consolidated regulation.\n\n## 15.
