   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis document covers the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) as the Commission's own page describes it, and a related Commission proposal that refers to it. The stored title, CSRD, names the Directive; the pool holds the Commission's explanatory page, last updated «This page was last updated on 9 December 2025», and the text of a different instrument, «COM(2023) 441 final 2023/0266(COD) Proposal for a REGULATION OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL on the accounting of greenhouse gas emissions of transport services». The pool holds no text of the Directive itself. The Directive's reach, per the Commission: «EU rules require large companies and listed companies to publish regular reports on the social and environmental risks they face, and on how their activities impact people and the environment.» What the sources say is quoted; what it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:*, and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe Commission describes the CSRD and its timing: «The first companies subject to the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) have to apply the new rules for the first time in the 2024 financial year, for reports published in 2025.» The standard to report under: «Companies subject to the CSRD have to report according to European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS).» The standards come from an outside body: «The standards are developed in a draft form by the EFRAG, previously known as the European Financial Reporting Advisory Group». The Directive reached the Official Journal on a stated date: «14 December 2022 Publication in the Official Journal - Corporate Sustainability Reporting Publication of the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) in the Official Journal». Later steps are dated on the page: «14 April 2025 Political agreement - “Stop‑the‑clock” Directive» for the stop-the-clock Directive, «11 July 2025 Adoption - ESRS Adoption of a “quick‑fix” delegated act» for the ESRS quick-fix, and «22 December 2023 Publication in the Official Journal» for the ESRS. Effective date as the page gives it: first application in the 2024 financial year.\n\nThe proposal ties the CSRD to transport: «may be used for corporate reporting, such under Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD)» and «The CSRD and this initiative are consistent in their approach». The two differ in subject: «the CSRD covers emissions of an entire company, and this Regulation covers emissions of transport services».\n\n*Analytical inference:* a freight business meets the CSRD as a supplier to customers that report under it, because the proposal says its transport service emissions data may feed those reports. This rests on the proposal sentences quoted above.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: the stop-the-clock Directive postpones wave two and wave three, and Omnibus I is a proposal with a political agreement whose terms the page does not state, so no reporting deadline for a freight business is dated in the pages held. The Commission records the latest step: «9 December 2025 Political agreement - Simplification omnibus Political agreement between the European Parliament and the Council on Omnibus I simplification package». The pool holds no later change.\n\n- A key-account lead asks each large or listed customer, at the next account review, whether it reports under the CSRD, for which financial year, and whether it expects to ask for transport emissions data, because the page records a postponement for some companies.\n- A data lead tests whether the shipment emissions the business gives customers can be produced on the EN ISO 14083:2023 method, because the Commission's proposal would make that standard the calculation method if adopted.\n- A contracts lead notes against each customer that is a wave two or wave three company that its first report was postponed by the stop-the-clock Directive, so it does not plan for a data request on the earlier timetable.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the three steps rest on the postponement, the Omnibus step and the proposal's method quoted in sections 2 and 8. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which wave a given customer falls in after the stop-the-clock Directive and Omnibus I, and whether the proposal has been adopted, which the pool does not state.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe sources name these roles: the reporting company, the EFRAG that drafts the standards, the Commission, and the European Parliament and Council that agreed the changes. The Commission's simplification aim reaches the value chain: «Moreover, it seeks to ensure that reporting requirements on large companies do not burden smaller companies in their value chains.» In the proposal the roles are the entity that calculates and discloses, the data intermediary and the conformity assessment body. Its scope: «This Regulation applies to any entity providing or organising freight and passenger services in the Union that calculates greenhouse gas emissions of a transport service starting or ending on the Union territory and discloses disaggregated information on those emissions to any third party for commercial or regulatory purposes.»\n\nThe CSRD page names no freight forwarder. The proposal's scope sentence reaches an entity that organises freight services and discloses calculated emissions to a third party.\n\n*Analytical inference:* a forwarder that organises freight and gives customers calculated shipment emissions would be within the proposal's scope if it were adopted as drafted, and sits under the CSRD only as a supplier to a reporting customer. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder is an entity organising freight services for that scope sentence, and the proposal's status.\n\n## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events\n\nSeveral steps are pending in the sources. The Commission records the simplification path: «the package proposes to apply the CSRD only to the largest companies (those with more than 1000 employees)» and the revised standards: «Public Consultation launched by EFRAG on revised ESRS exposure drafts . End date: 29 September 2025». The consultation has closed. For the transport proposal, the draft sets its own timing: «This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.» and «It shall apply from [ OP: Please insert a date: 42 months after the entry into force of this Regulation ].» A check follows: «The technical quality check is required as from 24 months after the date of the application of this Regulation , at the latest .»\n\n*Analytical inference:* if the 1000 employee line were adopted it would take companies below it out of direct CSRD reporting, and the proposal's application date is blank and depends on adoption; the pool does not say whether either has been adopted, so no calendar date is placed on the timeline for them.\n\n## 7. Threshold Questions\n\nThe threshold question for the CSRD is which company reports. The page says «large companies and listed companies» and gives the Omnibus proposal's line: «the package proposes to apply the CSRD only to the largest companies (those with more than 1000 employees)». It gives the waves: wave one reports first for the 2024 financial year, and «wave two and wave three companies» were postponed. For the proposal, the threshold is function: «This Regulation applies to any entity providing or organising freight and passenger services in the Union that calculates greenhouse gas emissions of a transport service starting or ending on the Union territory and discloses disaggregated information on those emissions to any third party for commercial or regulatory purposes.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a customer's reporting status depends on its size and wave, which the page gives only in outline. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the size and listing tests in the Directive's own text, which the pool does not hold.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nCSRD. «Companies subject to the CSRD have to report according to European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS).» The first reports: «The first companies subject to the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) have to apply the new rules for the first time in the 2024 financial year, for reports published in 2025.» Postponement: «postpones the entry into application of the reporting requirements for those companies that were previously required to report for the first time for financial years 2025 or 2026 (wave two and wave three companies).» Relief for wave one: «This revision gives additional flexibility in reporting to wave one companies and ensures that they do not have to report additional information for financial years 2025 and 2026 compared to what they had to report for financial 2024.» The page states no penalty.\n\nThe Commission proposal for transport services, which the pool holds as a proposal and not as adopted law, would require the following. Method: «defined in EN ISO 14083 :2023 standard , in its up-to-date version». Data: «the use of primary data for calculating greenhouse gas emissions of a transport service». Output: «The output data as a minimum shall consist total mass of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) per transport service, and, in relation to a type of transport service concerned, at least one of the following data metrics». Disclosure: «Concerned entities shall disclose output data in a clear and unambiguous manner». Verification: «Output data referred to in Article 9 shall be subject to verification of its conformity with the requirements laid down in Articles 4 to 9 of this Regulation.» Scope: «This Regulation applies to any entity providing or organising freight and passenger services in the Union». Exception: «with the exception of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises referred to in Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC».\n\n*Analytical inference:* the CSRD duties fall on the reporting company; the proposal's duties would fall on the entity that calculates and discloses, and the pool states no pass-through of any cost to a supplier or customer. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the current wave dates and scope after Omnibus I, and the proposal's status, none of which the pool states.\n\nNo phase-in is stated in Sections 4 to 6 of the proposal for the calculation, data and output rules.\n\nObligations surveyed: 8; workspace-adjacent: 3; extracted as FACT: 12.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nFor the CSRD the reporting duty is the published report under the ESRS, as quoted in section 8; the page names no registration. For the proposal, the verified output goes with proof: «Conformity assessment bodies shall be accredited to perform verification or certification activities referred to in Articles 11, 12 and 13.» and an entity «Concerned entities shall disclose output data in a clear and unambiguous manner». The pool states no filing by a forwarder under either instrument.\n\n*Analytical inference:* a reporting customer collects its own value chain data; a forwarder's duty to supply any of it comes only from contract unless the proposal is adopted. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a customer contract can require shipment-level emissions data.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the system work sits with reporting companies, and with calculating entities if the proposal is adopted. The Commission explains why, as the proposal puts it: «estimated that almost 600,000 entities in the EU transport sector measure their greenhouse gas emissions (2020), but only 21,660 of these do it at the disaggregated level needed to produce greenhouse gas emissions data of transport services.» The method behind the proposal is a published standard: «ISO published this new standard ISO 14083 :2023 in March 2023».\n\n*Analytical inference:* a forwarder that measures emissions at company or vehicle level, and not per shipment, is in the larger group the Commission describes and would need shipment-level calculation to give a customer service-level data; the proposal sets this as a duty only on an entity that discloses service-level emissions. *Legal Confirmation Required:* what a forwarder must change to meet the proposal if adopted.\n\n## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases\n\nOne exception is named. The proposal's verification applies to concerned entities «with the exception of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises referred to in Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC», and «The micro , small and medium-sized enterprises may undergo the verification upon their request.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a smaller forwarder that calculates and discloses emissions would be outside the mandatory verification but could choose it. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder qualifies as a micro, small or medium-sized enterprise on that Recommendation.\n\n## 13. Adjacent Industry Research and Alternatives\n\nThe method standard behind the proposal is ISO 14083, and the proposal's own statement of the problem is: «ISO published this new standard ISO 14083 :2023 in March 2023». The proposal says the CSRD and the new rules differ in subject: «the CSRD covers emissions of an entire company, and this Regulation covers emissions of transport services», and that the new data would help: «information generated from this initiative may contribute to companies’ general sustainability reports, thus facilitating the implementation of the CSRD».\n\n*Analytical inference:* ISO 14083 is the common method the proposal names; a forwarder that follows it would produce data a reporting customer can use in a CSRD report, if the customer chooses to. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any customer accepts ISO 14083 data for its own report.\n\n## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline\n\n- 14 December 2022: CSRD published in the Official Journal (past)\n- 22 December 2023: ESRS published in the Official Journal (past)\n- 14 April 2025: political agreement on the stop-the-clock Directive (past)\n- 11 July 2025: quick-fix delegated act on the ESRS adopted (past)\n- 29 September 2025: EFRAG consultation on revised ESRS exposure drafts closed (past)\n- 9 December 2025: political agreement on the Omnibus I simplification package (past)\n\n## 15.    "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis document covers the EU Emissions Trading System for shipping, which puts maritime emissions under the Union's carbon market, together with the reporting rules it builds on. The Commission's climate action page sets the scope: «Since January 2024, the EU's Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) has been extended to cover CO 2 emissions from all large ships (of 5 000 gross tonnage and above) entering EU ports, regardless of the flag they fly.» The law behind it is named on the page as «Directive (EU) 2023/959», an amendment to the ETS Directive, with the maritime reporting rules in «Regulation (EU) 2023/957». The captured texts hold the Commission's overview page and a data viewer page, not the text of that directive. They also hold the text of the FuelEU Maritime regulation and a proposal on transport emissions accounting, which are separate instruments; their dates and duties are not used here except where the overview page describes them. What the page says is stated from its own wording; what it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:* and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe regulation makes a ship's carbon dioxide emissions a cost: «In practice, shipping companies have to purchase and surrender (use) EU ETS emission allowances for each tonne of reported CO 2 (or CO 2 equivalent) emissions in the scope of the EU ETS system.» The share of emissions counted depends on the voyage: «50% of emissions from voyages starting or ending outside of the EU (allowing the third country to decide on appropriate action for the remaining share of emissions); 100% of emissions that occur between two EU ports and when ships are within EU ports.» Methane and nitrous oxide join later: «The EU ETS covers CO 2 (carbon dioxide), CH 4 (methane) and N 2 O (nitrous oxide) emissions, but the two latter only as from 2026.» The maritime emissions sit inside the same cap as other sectors: «Emissions from maritime transport are included in the overall ETS cap, which defines the maximum amount of greenhouse gases that can be emitted under the system.»\n\nThe page records when the regulation took effect: «These rules were adopted on 16 May 2023 and entered into force on 5 June 2023.» On the page, the party that buys and surrenders allowances is the shipping company. The page says the aim is to «incentivise energy efficiency, low-carbon solutions, and reductions of the price difference between alternative fuels and traditional maritime fuels».\n\n*Analytical inference:* a forwarder that books ocean legs calling at EU ports meets this rule through the carrier, whose allowance purchase is the stated cost; the page does not say whether or how a carrier passes it into a rate. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which party is the shipping company for a ship a client books, and whether the contract allows a charge for it.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nCOST ALERT: the allowance cost for maritime emissions is in force and the share to be surrendered rises. The page gives the steps: «2025: for 40% of their emissions reported in 2024; 2026: for 70% of their emissions reported in 2025; 2027 onwards: for 100% of their reported emissions». The page states no pass-through of this cost to carrier rates or surcharges, so whether a rate carries it is a gap.\n\n- A carrier-relations lead asks each ocean carrier in the rate agreements, at the next rate review, whether an EU ETS charge is added to rates for voyages touching an EU port and how its share of the carrier's emissions is worked out.\n- A pricing lead records, per ocean quote that includes a call at an EU port, which shipping company operates the ship and whether the quoted rate includes an allowance charge.\n\n*Analytical inference:* both steps rest on the duty to surrender allowances quoted above; the page requires neither of a forwarder. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any scheme cost may be charged by a carrier to a forwarder or its client under the business's contracts.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe page names these roles: the shipping company that buys and surrenders allowances, the administering authority of a Member State that ensures compliance, the accredited MRV shipping verifier, the flag State that receives emissions reports, and the Commission. It says «It is the role of administering authorities of EU Member States to ensure compliance using similar rules as for the other ETS sectors.» The shipping company is the party with the duty: «companies must – in line with their respective monitoring plans – monitor, for each of their ships, greenhouse gas emissions, fuel consumption and other parameters, such as distance travelled, time at sea and cargo carried on a per voyage basis, so as to gather annual data into an emissions report verified by an accredited MRV shipping verifier.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a forwarder, shipper or customs broker is not named, so on the page's text a business that only books space carries no allowance duty; the shipping company does. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which role the business holds if it charters a ship or runs its own, and whether the page's list of roles is complete in the directive text.\n\n## 5. Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis\n\nThe page lists guidance prepared with experts: «General guidance for shipping companies: the EU ETS and MRV Maritime (Guidance Document no. 1) General guidance on the process for approval of monitoring plans by administering authorities (Guidance Document no. 2) General guidance on accreditation and verification (Guidance Document no. 3)» It also lists FAQ pages on maritime transport in the EU ETS and on monitoring, reporting and verification.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the captured texts hold the titles of these guidance documents, not their content, so what they say about scope or reporting is not analysed here. *Legal Confirmation Required:* what Guidance Document no. 1 says about which company is responsible for a ship.\n\n## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events\n\nThe page names two forward points. The rules carry a review clause: «A reporting and review clause is included to monitor the implementation of the rules applicable to the maritime sector and to take into account relevant developments in the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).» And a global measure was due: «In July 2023 the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) made a step on this path committing to new targets for GHG emissions reductions and to develop and adopt in 2025 a basket of measure(s), delivering on these reduction targets.» The page does not say whether the IMO measures were adopted.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the review clause is where changes in the IMO's work can alter the maritime rules, and the 2025 date for the IMO measures is past, so the page does not tell what was decided. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the outcome of the IMO measures and any amendment to the maritime rules since the page was published.\n\n## 7. Threshold Questions\n\nTwo questions decide whether a voyage falls in the scheme. The first is ship size: «Since January 2024, the EU's Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) has been extended to cover CO 2 emissions from all large ships (of 5 000 gross tonnage and above) entering EU ports, regardless of the flag they fly.» The second is where the voyage runs: «50% of emissions from voyages starting or ending outside of the EU (allowing the third country to decide on appropriate action for the remaining share of emissions); 100% of emissions that occur between two EU ports and when ships are within EU ports.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a ship below 5 000 gross tonnage is outside the ETS coverage the page describes, and the share of a long-haul voyage that is counted is half of its emissions. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which share applies to a given route that mixes EU and non-EU ports.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nScope. «Since January 2024, the EU's Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) has been extended to cover CO 2 emissions from all large ships (of 5 000 gross tonnage and above) entering EU ports, regardless of the flag they fly.»\n\nShare counted. «50% of emissions from voyages starting or ending outside of the EU (allowing the third country to decide on appropriate action for the remaining share of emissions); 100% of emissions that occur between two EU ports and when ships are within EU ports.»\n\nGases and cap. «The EU ETS covers CO 2 (carbon dioxide), CH 4 (methane) and N 2 O (nitrous oxide) emissions, but the two latter only as from 2026.» «Emissions from maritime transport are included in the overall ETS cap, which defines the maximum amount of greenhouse gases that can be emitted under the system.»\n\nSurrender. «In practice, shipping companies have to purchase and surrender (use) EU ETS emission allowances for each tonne of reported CO 2 (or CO 2 equivalent) emissions in the scope of the EU ETS system.» «It is the role of administering authorities of EU Member States to ensure compliance using similar rules as for the other ETS sectors.»\n\nPhase-in. «To ensure a smooth transition, shipping companies only have to surrender allowances for a portion of their emissions during an initial phase-in period: 2025: for 40% of their emissions reported in 2024; 2026: for 70% of their emissions reported in 2025; 2027 onwards: for 100% of their reported emissions.» «The first surrendering deadline falls due in September 2025 in all Member States, in respect of emissions reported as taking place from 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2024.»\n\nMonitoring and reporting. «Monitoring: companies must – in line with their respective monitoring plans – monitor, for each of their ships, greenhouse gas emissions, fuel consumption and other parameters, such as distance travelled, time at sea and cargo carried on a per voyage basis, so as to gather annual data into an emissions report verified by an accredited MRV shipping verifier.» «by 30 April of each year (31 March as of 2025), companies must, through THETIS MRV , submit to the Commission and to the States in which those ships are registered» «As from 31 March 2025, emissions reports should also be submitted to the responsible administering authority trough THETIS-MRV.»\n\nDocument of compliance. «Document of compliance: by 30 June of each year, companies must ensure that all their ships that have performed activities in the previous reporting period and are visiting ports in the European Economic Area carry on board a document of compliance. This might be subject to inspections by Member States' authorities.»\n\nPenalty. The page states no penalty, fine or sanction for a missed surrender or a late report, so what a business risks if non-compliant is not stated. The page states no pass-through of allowance costs to carrier surcharges or freight rates.\n\n*Analytical inference:* each duty above falls on the shipping company; the page states no cost to a forwarder or to a customer of the shipping company. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any of these shipping company duties creates a charge or liability for a forwarder or its client.\n\nObligations surveyed: 8; workspace-adjacent: 3; extracted as FACT: 13.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nReports go through an EU system: «by 30 April of each year (31 March as of 2025), companies must, through THETIS MRV , submit to the Commission and to the States in which those ships are registered» And a second copy goes to the national authority: «As from 31 March 2025, emissions reports should also be submitted to the responsible administering authority trough THETIS-MRV.» The reporting rules started earlier: «Since 1 January 2018, large ships over 5 000 gross tonnage loading or unloading cargo or passengers at ports in the European Economic Area (EEA) must monitor and report related GHG emissions» The list of shipping companies and their administering authorities is kept up to date: «08/12/2025 – Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/2452 – Update to the list of shipping companies specifying the administering authority in respect of a shipping company». The data viewer from the European Environment Agency shows the scale: «The data reported under the EU emission trading system cover more than 16000 stationary installations, 1600 aircraft operators and 2600 maritime operators.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the reporting duties fall on the shipping company; the page states no report from a forwarder. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a business that operates ships is a company under the monitoring rules.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the system work sits with the shipping company, which must carry a document of compliance on board each ship. A procurement lead asks each ocean carrier, at contract renewal, to confirm in writing that the ships on the carrier's EU services carry a document of compliance for the previous reporting period, and files the answer with the carrier's record.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the step rests on the document of compliance sentence in section 8, which says inspections by Member States' authorities are possible; the page states no consequence for a forwarder if a ship has none. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder has any duty to check a carrier's document.\n\n## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases\n\nThe page lists special rules: «small islands and transnational routes under public service obligation or contract subject to specific provisions under the ETS Directive» It names the acts that set them: «Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/2895 of 19 December 2023 laying down the list of islands and ports referred to in Article 12(3-d) of Directive 2003/87/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and the list of transnational public service contracts or transnational public service obligations referred to in Article 12(3-c) of that Directive»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a service to a listed island or port, or a transnational public service route, may follow different ETS provisions from other EU calls. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a particular island or port call is on the Commission's list.\n\n## 13. Adjacent Industry Research and Alternatives\n\nThe page describes a sister measure on fuels: «A new FuelEU maritime Regulation to boost the demand for marine renewable and low-carbon fuels , by setting a maximum limit on the greenhouse gas content of energy used by ships calling at European ports and by encouraging zero-emission technology at berth (where ships stay in ports), with a technology-neutral approach;» This is a separate regulation from the ETS and has its own rules, which this document does not set out.\n\n*Analytical inference:* an ocean carrier may face both the allowance cost and a fuel rule, and the page does not say how the two interact. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the interaction of the two measures for a given ship.\n\n## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline\n\n- 1 January 2018: large ships over 5 000 gross tonnage calling at EEA ports start monitoring and reporting emissions (in force)\n- 16 May 2023: the rules were adopted (past)\n- 5 June 2023: the rules entered into force (in force)\n- January 2024: EU ETS extended to cover carbon dioxide emissions from large ships (in force)\n- 31 March 2025: emissions reports also go to the responsible administering authority (past)\n- September 2025: first surrendering deadline, for emissions reported for 2024 (past)\n- 2026: 70% of emissions reported in 2025 to be surrendered; methane and nitrous oxide covered from 2026 (current)\n- 2027: allowances for 100% of reported emissions from 2027 onwards (ahead)\n\n## 15.    "item_id": "956bad5c-80b0-411b-8fd5-726cc0d4a333",

   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis document covers California's Advanced Clean Trucks Regulation, set out in sections 1963 to 1963.5 of its final regulation order. Its stated purpose: «The purpose of sections 1963, 1963.1, 1963.2, 1963.3, 1963.4, and 1963.5 is to accelerate the market for on-road zero-emission vehicles and to reduce emissions of oxides of nitrogen (NOx), fine particulate matter (PM), other criteria pollutants, toxic air contaminants, and greenhouse gases (GHG) from medium- and heavy-duty on-road vehicles.» The jurisdiction is California, and the rule binds the maker of the vehicle, not the buyer or the carrier: «(b) Scope and Applicability. Any manufacturer that certifies on-road vehicles over 8,500 lbs. gross vehicle weight rating for sale in California is subject to sections 1963, 1963.1, 1963.2, 1963.3, 1963.4, and 1963.5 except as specified in section 1963(e).» What the order requires is stated from its own text; what it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:* and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe order is a credit-and-deficit system for new trucks. The general duty reads: «Except as provided in section 1963(e), a manufacturer must retire a number of ZEV or NZEV credits that equals or exceeds their total annual deficits each model year, subject to the provisions of section 1963.3.» The regulation enters into force for sales as a model-year step: its first deficits start with the 2024 model year. A deficit builds with sales: «Starting with the 2024 model year, a manufacturer shall annually incur deficits based on the manufacturer's annual sales volume of on- road vehicles produced and delivered for sale in California.» The deficit is set by a sales percentage schedule and a weight class modifier for each vehicle, and the order defines a manufacturer widely: «means any person who assembles new on-road motor vehicles, or imports such vehicles for resale, or who acts for and is under the control of any such person in connection with the distribution of new motor vehicles, but shall not include any dealer with respect to new motor vehicles received in commerce.»\n\nPlainly: a truck maker that sells new heavy vehicles into California has to show that a rising share of what it sells is zero-emission, or hold credits from those who sold more than the share required. The order places these duties on the manufacturer. A freight operator meets it as a buyer of new vehicles, or, if it brings new vehicles into California for resale, possibly as the manufacturer itself.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the order names no carrier, forwarder or fleet operator as a duty holder; the only party outside the maker it names is the ultimate purchaser, whose purchase sets when a deficit is incurred. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a business that imports a new on-road vehicle for resale falls within the manufacturer definition quoted above.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: the duties sit on manufacturers and the requirement is already in force, so no step falls on a freight operator within the next 30 days. A fleet purchasing lead who will be the ultimate purchaser of a new on-road vehicle for use in California asks the vehicle supplier, at the next purchase quote, whether the supplier is a manufacturer subject to the order or falls under the low volume exemption in section 1963(e), and records the answer in the supplier file.\n\n*Analytical inference:* this step rests on the exemption sentence in section 12 and on the deficit sentence in section 2, which tie the deficit to the sale to the ultimate purchaser; the order states no duty on the purchaser and no price effect of the schedule on a purchaser. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a supplier's exempt status changes anything for the buyer.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe order names these roles: the manufacturer, whose definition includes an importer of vehicles for resale; the ultimate purchaser in California; the Executive Officer of CARB, who receives reports and can audit; and the dealer, who is outside the manufacturer definition for new vehicles received in commerce. The definition of the maker reaches «This includes importers who import on-road vehicles for resale and persons that assemble glider vehicles.» The order also sets the party that carries the deficit: «Deficits are incurred when the on-road vehicle is sold to the ultimate purchaser in California.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a forwarder, carrier or customs broker is not named, so on the order's own text a business that only moves vehicles for others carries no manufacturer duty; a business that imports vehicles for resale is the case the order names. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which role a business holds for each vehicle it brings into California, including whether acting for an importer in distribution is within «who acts for and is under the control of any such person in connection with the distribution of new motor vehicles».\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nAnnual credit duty. «Except as provided in section 1963(e), a manufacturer must retire a number of ZEV or NZEV credits that equals or exceeds their total annual deficits each model year, subject to the provisions of section 1963.3.»\n\nDeficit and schedule. «Starting with the 2024 model year, a manufacturer shall annually incur deficits based on the manufacturer's annual sales volume of on- road vehicles produced and delivered for sale in California.» The schedule by model year is: «Table A-1. ZEV Sales Percentage Schedule Model Year Class 2b-3 Group Class 4-8 Group Class 7-8 Tractors Group 2024 5% 9% 5% 2025 7% 11% 7% 2026 10% 13% 10% 2027 15% 20% 15% 2028 20% 30% 20% 2029 25% 40% 25% 2030 30% 50% 30% 2031 35% 55% 35% 2032 40% 60% 40% 2033 45% 65% 40% 2034 50% 70% 40% 2035 and beyond 55% 75% 40%» In the table the Class 2b-3 Group, the Class 4-8 Group and the Class 7-8 Tractors Group each have their own sales percentage; the deficit for a vehicle is that percentage multiplied by a weight class modifier.\n\nMake-up. A maker that retires fewer credits than a model year requires «must make up the deficit by the end of the next model year by submitting a commensurate number of ZEV credits to satisfy the deficiency.» NZEV credits are capped: «A manufacturer may use NZEV credits to satisfy, at maximum, 50 percent of the annual summed deficits for the Class 2b-3 group and the Class 4-8 group, and may use Class 7-8 tractor NZEV credits to satisfy, at maximum, 50 percent of the annual summed deficits for the Class 7-8 tractor group.»\n\nCredit life. «ZEV or NZEV credits generated in the 2021, 2022 and 2023 model years expire at of the end of the 2030 model year, and are no longer available to be used to meet compliance for 2031 and later model years.» «ZEV or NZEV credits generated in 2024 and subsequent model years may be used only for five model years after the model year in which they are generated.»\n\nNear-zero-emission range. «NZEVs must have an all- electric range that equals or exceeds the criteria specified in 17 CCR section 95663(d) until the end of the 2029 model year and an all-electric range that equals or exceeds 75 miles or greater starting with the 2030 model year.»\n\nScope. «(b) Scope and Applicability. Any manufacturer that certifies on-road vehicles over 8,500 lbs. gross vehicle weight rating for sale in California is subject to sections 1963, 1963.1, 1963.2, 1963.3, 1963.4, and 1963.5 except as specified in section 1963(e).»\n\nPenalty. «Any manufacturer that fails to retire an appropriate amount of ZEV or NZEV credits as specified in section 1963.3(c) and does not make up deficits within the specified time allowed by section 1963.3(b) shall be subject to Health and Safety Code section 43212 civil penalty applicable to a manufacturer who does not comply with emission standards or the test procedures adopted by the state board.» «For the purposes of Health and Safety Code section 43212, the number of vehicles not meeting the state board's standards or procedures shall be equal to one half of the manufacturer’s outstanding deficit.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* each duty above falls on the manufacturer; the order states no sales price, surcharge or other cost to a vehicle buyer, so any effect on what a fleet pays rests on a link the text does not give. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any of these manufacturer duties reaches a business that imports vehicles for resale, and how the penalty count applies to it.\n\nObligations surveyed: 7; workspace-adjacent: 0; extracted as FACT: 13.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nReporting is annual and follows each model year: «Beginning with the 2021 model year, and no later than 90 days following the end of each model year, a manufacturer must report the following information to CARB for each on-road vehicle produced and delivered for sale in California for each model year» Credit trades are reported too: «Reports must be submitted no later than 90 days following the end of each model year to demonstrate compliance.» Records are kept for years: «Records of reported information required in section 1963.4 and documentation showing vehicle delivery to the ultimate purchaser at a location in California must be kept by manufacturers for CARB to audit for a period of eight (8) years from the end of the model year the vehicles were produced.» CARB can audit: «A manufacturer must make records of vehicle sales into California available to the Executive Officer within 30 days of a request for audit to verify the accuracy of the reported information.»\n\nThe order sets no registration step beyond these reports and records.\n\n*Analytical inference:* these reports are made by manufacturers to CARB; the text asks for none from a forwarder or carrier. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a business that imports vehicles for resale would have to file the sales report in its own name.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the system work sits with manufacturers: the sales report lists the vehicle identification number, weight class, fuel and drivetrain type and volume for each vehicle, and the records must be kept so CARB can audit them. A compliance lead at a business that imports new on-road vehicles for resale checks, before the next import into California, whether the business can produce a vehicle identification number list and delivery records for each vehicle, since the order asks for exactly those records from a manufacturer.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the step rests on the reporting and record sentences in section 10; it applies only if the business is a manufacturer under the definition in section 2. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the business is a manufacturer for these vehicles.\n\n## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases\n\nSmall makers are exempt: «Each model year, starting in 2024, manufacturers that do not exceed 500 average annual sales of on-road vehicles produced and delivered for sale in California for the three prior model years are exempt from the requirements of sections 1963 through 1963.5.» An exempt maker can still opt in: «Any manufacturer that is exempt may elect to generate ZEV or NZEV credits per the provisions of section 1963.2.» A maker that grows past the limit comes in: «Manufacturers that meet this exemption as of 2021 but subsequently exceed 500 average annual vehicle sales in any model year become subject to the requirements of sections 1963 through 1963.5 starting the second model year after the average annual sales exceeded the threshold.» Some buses are outside the vehicle definition: «Is not an excluded bus as defined in section 1963(c)(11).»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the low volume exemption turns on average annual sales of on-road vehicles for sale in California over the three prior model years, so a business near the limit cannot tell its status from a single year. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a particular maker or importer meets the exemption conditions for a given model year.\n\n## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline\n\n- 2021: credit generation, banking and trading rules and sales reporting begin with the 2021 model year (in force)\n- 2024: first model year of deficits, with sales percentages of 5% (Class 2b-3), 9% (Class 4-8) and 5% (Class 7-8 tractors), and the start of the low volume exemption (in force)\n- 2027: sales percentages of 15%, 20% and 15%\n- 2030: electric range minimum of 75 miles for near-zero-emission credit starts with the 2030 model year; credits from the 2021 to 2023 model years expire at the end of the 2030 model year\n- 2032: sales percentages of 40%, 60% and 40%\n- 2035: sales percentages of 55%, 75% and 40% for 2035 and beyond; near-zero-emission credits can be generated only until the end of the 2035 model year\n\n## 15.    "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis brief covers The Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016, a United Kingdom statutory instrument published on legislation.gov.uk. It is headed: «The Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016 Made 11th December 2016 Coming into force in accordance with regulation 1(1)»\n\nWhere it reaches: «These Regulations extend to England and Wales only. (3) They apply in relation to— (a) England and the sea adjacent to England out as far as the seaward boundary of the territorial sea, and (b) Wales,»\n\nThe Regulations set up one permit system for many kinds of site activity. What they require is quoted from their own text. What it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:*, and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*. A freight forwarder is not named in the Regulations.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe Regulations decide which activities need an environmental permit and make it an offence to run them without one. The activities are listed as regulated facilities: «In these Regulations, “ regulated facility ” means any of the following— (a) an installation; (b) mobile plant; (c) a waste operation; (d) a mining waste operation; (e) a radioactive substances activity; (f) a water discharge activity; (g) a groundwater activity; (h) a small waste incineration plant; (i) a solvent emission activity; (j) a flood risk activity. [ F46 (k) a medium combustion plant; (l) a specified generator ]»\n\nThe core rule is: «A person must not, except under and to the extent authorised by an environmental permit— (a) operate a regulated facility, or (b) cause or knowingly permit a water discharge activity or groundwater activity.»\n\nWhen the Regulations take effect: «These Regulations may be cited as the Environmental Permitting (England and Wales) Regulations 2016 and come into force 21 days after the day on which these Regulations are made.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a business reaches the Regulations when it runs, or lets someone run for it, one of these activities at a site in England or Wales, for example a combustion plant or a waste operation; a business with no such activity at such a site is not within the permit rule.\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a given site activity is a regulated facility and which class it falls in.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: the permit rule for existing medium combustion plant of 5 megawatts or less starts on 1st January 2029, a step ahead that binds the operator of a site with such a plant, and for existing plant above 5 megawatts it started on 1st January 2024. Both dates are quoted in section 8.\n\n- A site operations lead, at the next review of each site, lists every site in England or Wales that the business operates, each combustion plant with its rated thermal input and the date it was put into operation, and marks every plant of 1 megawatt or more but less than 50 megawatts that was put into operation before 20th December 2018; each marked plant of 5 megawatts or less comes inside the permit rule on 1st January 2029, and each above 5 megawatts came inside it on 1st January 2024.\n- A procurement lead asks each third-party site operator in England or Wales that the business books cargo through, at each new booking, to state in writing which environmental permit covers the activities at the site, because a person who knowingly causes or permits a contravention is also within the offence quoted in section 4.\n\n*Analytical inference:* the first step rests on the thresholds and dates in sections 7 and 8; the second rests on the offence in section 4. The Regulations name no forwarder duty. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether booking cargo through a site is causing or knowingly permitting a contravention by its operator.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe Regulations place the permit duty on the operator, the person in control of the facility. «“ operator ”, in relation to a regulated facility, means— (a) the person who has control over the operation of the regulated facility, (b) if the regulated facility has not yet been put into operation, the person who will have control over the regulated facility when it is put into operation»\n\nThe offence also reaches those who cause or permit: «It is an offence for a person to— (a) contravene regulation 12(1), or (b) knowingly cause or knowingly permit the contravention of regulation 12(1)(a).» And a second person can be liable: «If an offence committed by a person under this regulation is due to the act or default of some other person, that other person is also guilty of the offence and liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly, whether or not proceedings for the offence are taken against the first-mentioned person.»\n\nThe regulator is set by place: «functions in relation to a regulated facility that is or will be operated in England are exercisable by the Agency; (b) functions in relation to a regulated facility that is or will be operated in Wales are exercisable by the NRBW»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a client or site operator that controls a plant is the operator; a forwarder is within the Regulations only if it controls a facility or knowingly causes or permits a contravention. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which party is the operator of a shared site and whether a booking arrangement amounts to causing or permitting.\n\n## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events\n\nThe Regulations require the Secretary of State to review them: «The first report under this regulation must be published before the end of December 2019.» «Subsequent reports under this regulation must be published at intervals not exceeding 5 years.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the review reports are reviews of the Regulations by the Secretary of State for England; they set no date for a freight business. The first report date has passed.\n\n## 7. Threshold Questions\n\nThe threshold that decides whether a combustion plant is inside the permit rule is its rated thermal input. «“medium combustion plant” means a combustion plant with a rated thermal input equal to or greater than 1 megawatt but less than 50 megawatts, and any combination of combustion plants referred to in article 2(2) or article 4 of the MCPD, provided that—»\n\nAn existing plant is one already running by a cut-off date: «“existing medium combustion plant” means a medium combustion plant— (a) put into operation before 20th December 2018, or (b) for which an environmental permit was granted before 19th December 2017, provided that the plant is put into operation no later than 20th December 2018»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a plant below 1 megawatt or at 50 megawatts or above is not a medium combustion plant by this definition; plants above or below the limits may still fall under another class of regulated facility. *Legal Confirmation Required:* how the rated thermal input of several plants at one site is combined under the definition.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nPermit rule. The rule in section 2 has its own carve-out for radioactive substances: «In respect of a radioactive substances activity, paragraph (1) does not apply to a person to whom a radioactive substances exemption applies for that activity.»\n\nStaged start for medium combustion plant. The permit rule is switched on in steps: «Paragraph (1)(a) does not apply in relation to the operation of a medium combustion plant, mobile medium combustion plant or a specified generator comprising— (a) a new medium combustion plant, before 20th December 2018;» «(b) an existing medium combustion plant with a rated thermal input greater than 5 megawatts, before 1st January 2024;» «(c) an existing medium combustion plant with a rated thermal input of less than or equal to 5 megawatts, before 1st January 2029;»\n\nOffences. «It is an offence for a person to fail to comply with or to contravene an environmental permit condition.» «But it is not an offence for a person to fail to comply with the environmental permit conditions in Part 3 of Schedule 9 (waste operations: management and technical competence conditions).» «It is an offence for a person to fail to comply with the requirements of an enforcement notice or of a prohibition notice, suspension notice, landfill closure notice, mining waste facility closure notice, flood risk activity emergency works notice or flood risk activity remediation notice.»\n\nPenalties. «a person guilty of an offence under regulation 38(1), (2) or (3) is liable— (a) on summary conviction to a fine or imprisonment for a term not exceeding [ F72 the general limit in a magistrates’ court ] , or to both; (b) on conviction on indictment to a fine or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 5 years, or to both.» «A person guilty of an offence under regulation 38(4) is liable— (a) on summary conviction to a fine; (b) on conviction on indictment to a fine or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 2 years, or to both.»\n\nEmission limits. «From 1st January 2025, emission limit values applicable to an existing medium combustion plant with a rated thermal input greater than 5 megawatts, for emissions into the air of sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and dust, are the corresponding emission limit values set out in Tables 2 and 3 of Part 1 of Annex II.» «From 1st January 2030, emission limit values applicable to an existing medium combustion plant with a rated thermal input of less than or equal to 5 megawatts, for emissions into the air of sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and dust, are the corresponding emission limit values set out in Tables 1 and 3 of Part 1 of Annex II.»\n\nRegulator powers. «If the regulator considers that an operator has contravened, is contravening, or is likely to contravene an environmental permit condition, the regulator may serve a notice on the operator.» «The regulator may suspend an environmental permit by serving a notice (a “suspension notice”) on the operator under this regulation.» «The Agency may by notice impose on a person a requirement to pay to the Agency a monetary penalty of such amount as the Agency may determine (“a variable monetary penalty”) in relation to a relevant offence which is committed in England on or after 1st December 2023.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* each duty above is placed on the operator or on the person who commits the offence; the Regulations state no price or charge to a customer. The staged dates mean a site with an existing medium combustion plant of 5 megawatts or less has until the 2029 date, while a larger one is already inside the rule.\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any site a client or the business uses is an existing medium combustion plant site and which of the staged dates applies to it.\n\nObligations surveyed: 7; workspace-adjacent: 3; extracted as FACT: 14.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nThe regulator may demand information from any person: «an appropriate authority, regulator, exemption registration authority or exemption authority, by notice served on any person, may require that person to provide such information in such form and within such period as is specified in the notice.» Giving false information or false records is an offence: «(c) intentionally to make a false entry in a record required to be kept under an environmental permit condition;»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a business that supplies information or keeps records for a permitted site must keep them true; the Regulations name no registration step for a forwarder. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a client may require a forwarder to supply records for a site under a permit condition.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the Regulations require no system of a freight forwarder, and the work ahead falls on sites with a permit or a plant that needs one. An operations lead asks each site operator the business uses in England or Wales how the site records are kept for the permit and who answers a notice from the regulator, before the 2029 date in section 3.\n\nA notice must state what to fix and by when: «(c) specify the steps that must be taken to remedy the contravention or to ensure that the likely contravention does not occur, and (d) specify the period within which those steps must be taken.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* an enforcement notice sets steps and a period, so a site that cannot show its permit records quickly is slower to answer it. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that stores records for a client must make them available to a regulator.\n\n## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases\n\nSome activities and facilities are outside the permit rule. «But the following are not regulated facilities— (a) an exempt facility; (b) an excluded waste operation; (c) the disposal or recovery of household waste from a domestic property within the curtilage of that property by a person other than an establishment or undertaking;» Exempt facilities are carved out of the water rule: «(2) Paragraph (1)(b) does not apply if the water discharge activity or groundwater activity is an exempt facility.»\n\nAn emergency defence exists: «It is a defence for a person charged with an offence under regulation 38(1), (2) or (3) to prove that the acts alleged to constitute the contravention were done in an emergency in order to avoid danger to human health in a case where— (a) the person took all such steps as were reasonably practicable in the circumstances for minimising pollution, and (b) particulars of the acts were furnished to the regulator as soon as reasonably practicable after they were done.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the defence needs both steps, minimising pollution and telling the regulator, and covers only the offences in regulation 38(1), (2) or (3). *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a particular activity at a client site is an exempt facility.\n\n## 14.    "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis brief covers the United States Environmental Protection Agency rule «Greenhouse Gas Emissions Standards for Heavy-Duty Vehicles--Phase 3; Final Rule» It was published in the Federal Register as: «[Federal Register Volume 89, Number 78 (Monday, April 22, 2024)] [Rules and Regulations] [Pages 29440-29831]» The agency's rule page says: «On March 29, 2024, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced a final rule, “Greenhouse Gas Emissions Standards for Heavy-Duty Vehicles – Phase 3,” that sets stronger standards to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from heavy-duty (HD) vehicles beginning in model year (MY) 2027.»\n\nWho it reaches: «This action relates to companies that manufacture, sell, or import into the United States new heavy-duty highway vehicles and engines. This action also relates to state and local governments.»\n\nStatus flag. The same agency page lists, under related information, two later items: «Final Rule: Rescission of the Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding and Motor Vehicle Greenhouse Gas Emission Standards Under the Clean Air Act» and «EPA Announces Action to Implement POTUS’s Termination of Biden-Harris Electric Vehicle Mandate» The text read here does not state what these items do to the Phase 3 standards, so the dates below are the dates of the 2024 rule, as of «Last updated on July 9, 2026».\n\nWhat the rule requires is quoted from its own text. What it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:*, and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*. A freight forwarder is not named in the text read here.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe rule sets carbon dioxide limits on new heavy trucks and tractors, and the scope sentence in section 1 names the companies that manufacture, sell or import those vehicles.    "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document\n\nThis brief covers the European Union regulation on the classification, labelling and packaging of chemical substances and mixtures, known as CLP: «Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008 on classification, labelling and packaging of substances and mixtures, amending and repealing Directives 67/548/EEC and 1999/45/EC, and amending Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (Text with EEA relevance)» It was published as: «Official Journal L 353 , 31/12/2008 P. 0001 - 1355»\n\nIts aim: «(1) This Regulation should ensure a high level of protection of human health and the environment as well as the free movement of chemical substances, mixtures and certain specific articles, while enhancing competitiveness and innovation.» Its reach: «(b) providing an obligation for: (i) manufacturers, importers and downstream users to classify substances and mixtures placed on the market; (ii) suppliers to label and package substances and mixtures placed on the market;» It is binding across the Union: «This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.»\n\nThe text read here is the Regulation as published in 2008. What it requires is quoted from its own text. What it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:*, and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*. A freight forwarder is not named in the Regulation. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the 2008 text read here has been amended since publication.\n\n## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace\n\nThe Regulation makes the people who put hazardous chemicals on the EU market classify them, label them and pack them to a common standard. Who counts as a supplier: «\"supplier\" means any manufacturer, importer, downstream user or distributor placing on the market a substance, on its own or in a mixture, or a mixture;» What counts as placing on the market: «\"placing on the market\" means supplying or making available, whether in return for payment or free of charge, to a third party. Import shall be deemed to be placing on the market;»\n\nWhen it takes effect: «This Regulation shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.» The Regulation enters into force on that day, and its main titles apply later: «Titles II, III and IV shall apply in respect of substances from 1 December 2010 and in respect of mixtures from 1 June 2015.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a business that imports hazardous substances or mixtures, or hands them on, meets the Regulation as an importer, a downstream user or a distributor; a business that only moves goods under the transport rules meets it mainly through Article 33 in section 7.\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a business that imports or hands on hazardous goods is an importer, downstream user or distributor under the definitions quoted.\n\n## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action\n\nMONITORING: every date in the Regulation has passed, so there is no new step, and what remains is a standing check on labels that a forwarder meets in practice.\n\n- A dangerous-goods compliance lead asks each client that supplies hazardous substances or mixtures for the Union, at its next booking review, to confirm in writing that the inner and any intermediate packaging is labelled under this Regulation where the outer packaging carries the transport dangerous goods label, because Article 33(1) requires the inner label (section 7).\n- A documentation lead, at each new booking, records for each Member State a client ships into, the official language(s) of that State and asks the client to confirm the label is written in it, because Article 17(2) sets that rule unless the Member State provides otherwise (section 8).\n\n*Analytical inference:* both steps rest on the Article 33 and Article 17 spans quoted in sections 7 and 8; the Regulation puts the labelling duty on the supplier, not on a forwarder. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a business that packs, repacks or relabels goods for a client is itself a supplier under the definitions in section 2.\n\n## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain\n\nThe Regulation names manufacturers, importers, downstream users, distributors and suppliers, and a freight forwarder is not among them. Who is an importer: «\"importer\" means any natural or legal person established within the Community who is responsible for import;» What import is: «\"import\" means the physical introduction into the customs territory of the Community;» A distributor is: «\"distributor\" means any natural or legal person established within the Community, including a retailer, who only stores and places on the market a substance, on its own or in a mixture, for third parties;»\n\nSuppliers share the work: «Suppliers in a supply chain shall cooperate to meet the requirements for classification, labelling and packaging in this Regulation.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a forwarder that is established in the Union and is responsible for import would be an importer, and an importer places goods on the market on import; a forwarder that only carries goods for another party is not named in these definitions. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder acting for a client is responsible for import within the definition, and which party is then the supplier for labelling.\n\n## 7. Threshold Questions\n\nThe threshold question for a freight business is whether the transport rules or this Regulation govern a package. The exclusion: «Save where Article 33 applies this Regulation shall not apply to the transport of dangerous goods by air, sea, road, rail or inland waterways.» Where an outer package meets the transport labelling rules: «Where a package consists of an outer and an inner packaging, together with any intermediate packaging, and the outer packaging meets labelling provisions in accordance with the rules on the transport of dangerous goods, the inner and any intermediate packaging shall be labelled in accordance with this Regulation.» Where it does not: «Where the outer packaging of a package is not required to meet labelling provisions in accordance with rules on the transport of dangerous goods, both the outer and any inner packaging, including any intermediate packaging, shall be labelled in accordance with this Regulation. However, if the outer packaging permits the inner or intermediate packaging labelling to be clearly seen, the outer packaging need not be labelled.» And for a single package: «Single packages that meet the labelling provisions in accordance with the rules on the transport of dangerous goods shall be labelled both in accordance with this Regulation and the rules on the transport of dangerous goods.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the transport exclusion does not remove the inner and intermediate packaging from this Regulation when Article 33 applies; the label on the outer package for transport and the label on the inner package under this Regulation are separate duties. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which rule governs a given package and who must label the inner packaging.\n\n## 8. Substantive Requirements\n\nClassify before selling. «Manufacturers, importers and downstream users shall classify substances or mixtures in accordance with Title II before placing them on the market.» «Where a substance or mixture is classified as hazardous, suppliers shall ensure that the substance or mixture is labelled and packaged in accordance with Titles III and IV, before placing it on the market.» «Substances and mixtures shall not be placed on the market unless they comply with this Regulation.»\n\nLabel content and language. «A substance or mixture classified as hazardous and contained in packaging shall bear a label including the following elements: (a) the name, address and telephone number of the supplier(s);» «The label shall be written in the official language(s) of the Member State(s) where the substance or mixture is placed on the market, unless the Member State(s) concerned provide(s) otherwise.»\n\nUpdating labels. «The supplier shall ensure that the label is updated, without undue delay, following any change to the classification and labelling of that substance or mixture, where the new hazard is more severe or where new supplemental labelling elements are required under Article 25» «Where labelling changes are required other than those referred to in paragraph 1, the supplier shall ensure that the label is updated within 18 months.»\n\nPackages for transport. The Article 33 rules are in section 7.\n\nScope exclusions. «This Regulation shall not apply to the following: (a) radioactive substances and mixtures within the scope of Council Directive 96/29/Euratom of 13 May 1996» «Member States may allow for exemptions from this Regulation in specific cases for certain substances or mixtures, where necessary in the interests of defence.»\n\nPenalties. «Member States shall introduce penalties for non-compliance with this Regulation and shall take all measures necessary to ensure that this Regulation is applied. The penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.» «Member States shall notify the Commission of the provisions for penalties by 20 June 2010 and shall notify it without delay of any subsequent amendment affecting them.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* each duty above is placed on the manufacturer, importer, downstream user or supplier named; none is placed on a forwarder, and the Regulation states no charge to a customer. No phase-in is stated in Articles 4, 17, 30 and 33 beyond the application dates in section 14.\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a penalty or a duty on a supplier can reach a forwarder that tenders a mislabelled package, and what the penalties are in each Member State.\n\nObligations surveyed: 8; workspace-adjacent: 3; extracted as FACT: 11.\n\n## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations\n\nManufacturers and importers must notify the Agency. The duty: «Any manufacturer or importer, or group of manufacturers or importers (hereinafter referred to as \"the notifier(s)\"), who places on the market a substance referred to in Article 39, shall notify to the Agency the following information in order for it to be included in the inventory referred to in Article 42:» The timing: «Substances placed on the market on or after 1 December 2010 shall be notified in accordance with paragraph 1 within one month after their placing on the market.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* the notification duty falls on manufacturers and importers that place a substance on the market; the Regulation names no registration or notification for a forwarder. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that is an importer of substances must notify.\n\n## 11. Operational System Requirements\n\nMONITORING: the Regulation builds no system for a freight forwarder. A product-data lead, at each new booking, keeps for each client's hazardous product the label date and classification date, and asks the client to send a revised label when the classification changes, because the supplier must update labels on a stated clock: «The supplier shall ensure that the label is updated, without undue delay, following any change to the classification and labelling of that substance or mixture, where the new hazard is more severe or where new supplemental labelling elements are required under Article 25, taking into account the nature of the change as regards the protection of human health and the environment. Suppliers shall cooperate in accordance with Article 4(9) to complete the changes to the labelling without undue delay. 2. Where labelling changes are required other than those referred to in paragraph 1, the supplier shall ensure that the label is updated within 18 months.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* a package already in the chain may carry an older label than the current classification, so the date of the label is the fact to record. *Legal Confirmation Required:* what a forwarder must do on receiving a package whose label predates a classification change.\n\n## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases\n\nSeveral edge cases are stated. In transit: «(b) substances and mixtures which are subject to customs supervision, provided that they do not undergo any treatment or processing, and which are in temporary storage, or in a free zone or free warehouse with a view to re-exportation, or in transit;» Small packages: «Where the packaging of a substance or a mixture is either in such a shape or form or is so small that it is impossible to meet the requirements of Article 31 for a label in the languages of the Member State in which the substance or mixture is placed on the market, the label elements in accordance with the first subparagraph of Article 17(2) shall be provided in accordance with section 1.5.1 of Annex I.»\n\n*Analytical inference:* goods held under customs supervision in transit or temporary storage, without treatment or processing, are outside the Regulation for that stage; a package too small for the full label may carry reduced label information as the cited annex section allows. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether goods in a free warehouse or in transit meet the conditions of the exclusion.\n\n## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline\n\n- 16 December 2008: the Regulation is adopted; «Done at Strasbourg, 16 December 2008.»\n- 20 June 2010: Member States were to notify the Commission of their penalty provisions (past)\n- 1 December 2010: Titles II, III and IV apply to substances (past); until then substances follow Directive 67/548/EEC under Article 61\n- 20 January 2012: the Agency study and the Commission review in the Regulation were due (past); «By 20 January 2012, the Agency shall carry out a study on the communication of information to the general public on the safe use of substances and mixtures»\n- 1 January 2014: tests for physical hazards must meet a recognised quality system from this date (past); «Where new tests for physical hazards are carried out for the purposes of this Regulation, they shall be carried out, at the latest from 1 January 2014, in compliance with a relevant recognised quality system or by laboratories complying with a relevant recognised standard.»\n- 1 June 2015: Titles II, III and IV apply to mixtures and the two earlier directives are repealed (past); «Directive 67/548/EEC and Directive 1999/45/EC shall be repealed with effect from 1 June 2015.»\n*Analytical inference:* every dated step has passed; the standing duties in section 8 continue.\n\n*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether later amendments of the 2008 text move any date above.\n\n## 15. Sources\n\n- Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008 on classification, labelling and packaging of substances and mixtures, Official Journal of the European Union, L 353: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32008R1272\n",

    "what_is_it": "Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008, published in Official Journal L 353 on 31/12/2008, is the European Union regulation on classification, labelling and packaging of substances and mixtures. It obliges manufacturers, importers and downstream users to classify, and suppliers to label and package, and Member States set the penalties.",
    "why_matters": "The transport exclusion in Article 1(6) does not apply where Article 33 applies, so the inner and any intermediate packaging of a hazardous product must be labelled under this Regulation even when the outer package carries the transport dangerous goods label. The label must be in the official language(s) of the Member State where the product is placed on the market, and a supplier must update it without undue delay after a more severe classification and within 18 months for other changes. Penalties are set by Member States and the Regulation states none itself, so exposure for a mislabelled package depends on national law.",
    "what_it_changes": "Inner and intermediate packaging needs a CLP label even under transport rules; labels follow the market's language; penalties are national and the Regulation names no forwarder duty.",

   "claims": [

     "claim_kind": "FACT",
     "claim_text": "The Regulation is Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 of 16 December 2008 on classification, labelling and packaging of substances and mixtures.",
     "source_span": "Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008 on classification, labelling and packaging of substances and mixtures, amending and repealing Directives 67/548/EEC and 1999/45/EC, and amending Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (Text with EEA relevance)",

    },
    {

     "claim_text": "It appears in Official Journal L 353, 31/12/2008, pages 0001 to 1355.",
     "source_span": "Official Journal L 353 , 31/12/2008 P. 0001 - 1355",
